speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my question is to the Minister of Employment and Immigration.
The minister will know that the Canadian Human Rights Act was passed by this parliament and that it applies explicitly to all government departments and agencies. He will also know that he, or his officials on his instructions are now asking the Federal Court of Canada to declare that the Human Rights Commission has no jurisdiction over his department and over the dealings of his department with the millions of people who come to this country each year.
Will the minister tell the House on what grounds he can justify his position that the Human Rights Act applies to everybody else but not to his department?

subsubtopic: INCREASE IN DIVIDEND PAYMENTS TO FOREIGN COMPANIES- EFFECT ON GNP
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have a question for the President of the Board of Economic Development Ministers.
Statistics Canada figures released just a few hours ago show that gross national product increases in 1978 were at an alarmingly low level of only 3.4 per cent, well below what the Minister of Finance forecast. Statistics Canada points out that this has been largely due to the significant increase in the outflow of dividend payments to countries outside Canada, that profits were up by 24 per cent and that dividend payments going out increased to $2.2 billion. Statistics Canada states that price increases have been unusually large.
Would the minister not agree that in ordinary language this means that foreign-owned firms are overcharging Canadians
February 27, 1979

and taking excessive profits out of this country and into others?

speakeroldname: Hon. Robert K. Andras (President of the Board of Economic Development Ministers):
speakerposition: Minister of State for Economic Development
subsubtopic: INCREASE IN DIVIDEND PAYMENTS TO FOREIGN COMPANIES- EFFECT ON GNP
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we will have a debate this afternoon on the whole subject of inflation. I have not seen the evidence of excessive profits to which the hon. member is referring, whether they be excessive profits in the hands of Canadian-owned corporations or foreign corporations.
I had some difficulty with the arithmetic at the beginning of the hon. member's question. He was talking about a 3.4 per cent growth in the gross national product and he said that that was attributable to the passage of dividends from Canada to foreign countries. I am really at a bit of a loss to understand what his reference was, but on the general subject I do not think the premise on which the hon. member based his question is actually accurate.

subsubtopic: INCREASE IN DIVIDEND PAYMENTS TO FOREIGN COMPANIES- EFFECT ON GNP
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I hope before the debate takes place at three o'clock the minister will have a chance to look at these truly alarming figures. They were released publicly just a few hours ago and they point out that profits were up about 24 per cent, year over year, for 1978. They point out that there was a $2.2 billion flow of dividend payments outside the country. These are facts and they are connected.
Almost 60 per cent of Canadian manufacturing is owned by companies with head offices outside Canada. I would like to ask the minister, given the serious economic consequences of this situation and the Prime Minister's own promise to do something about it back in 1974, when will the government be prepared to implement that promise as it pertains to resource ownership in this country?

speakerposition: Minister of State for Economic Development
subsubtopic: INCREASE IN DIVIDEND PAYMENTS TO FOREIGN COMPANIES- EFFECT ON GNP
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I know the hon. member has said on other occasions that his party would espouse a policy of controlling the flow of capital outside this country. This is one of his answers to the passage of dividends, or anything else I supppose, outside Canada. In my view, that would be the most destructive policy possible for a country that depends for 25 per cent of its gross national product on export and on trading, because it would totally isolate this country from trade back and forth between nations. I think it would be an outrageous and disastrous policy to espouse.
There are many developmental programs in trade now working in consultation with the private sector to increase our GNP, to increase our export competitiveness, and indeed this involves talking to multinational corporations to see that they honour the principles of corporate responsibility within this country, and I am encouraged by the response we are getting.

speechtext:
My question centres on the gross national product figures just released. First, has the minister read these rather alarming figures? Second, in view of the fact the fourth quarter GNP now is seasonally adjusted at an annual rate of only 1.8 per cent, only 3.4 per cent for the entire year last year, would the minister indicate why the Minister of Finance predicted only last November that the real growth would be 4.5 per cent? would achieve 5 per cent real growth in the country, when the record has been so dismal?

speakeroldname: Hon. Robert K. Andras (President of the Board of Economic Development Ministers):
speakerposition: Minister of State for Economic Development
subsubtopic: GROWTH OF GNP BELOW THAT FORECAST BY GOVERNMENT-REASON THEREFOR

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to direct a question to the Minister of Justice, having in mind the facts set out in the reasons for judgment given by the Quebec Court of Appeal.
In light of the fact the Minister of Supply and Services, quite honestly and openly, said in the House that he had some doubts as to the security procedure which must have been used in the case of Dr. Treu, that in this particular case prosecutions could be launched only under the direct order of the Attorney General, and that the prosecution launched was directed toward an indictable offence, is the minister prepared to review the facts in this case and give consideration to the provision of some form of compensation for Dr. Alexander Peter Treu?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada; Minister responsible for the Status of Women
subsubtopic: COMPENSATION FOR PETER TREU-MINISTER'S POSITION
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I have reviewed all the facts in this case very carefully. Also, I read the judgment of the Court of Appeal very carefully. I would remind the hon. member that the principle of making ex gratia payments to persons accused of criminal offences who are acquitted, whether at the trial level or on appeal, is not a principle which is part of criminal justice in Canada.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subsubtopic: COMPENSATION FOR PETER TREU-MINISTER'S POSITION
speechtext: Ask Jean-Pierre Goyer.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada; Minister responsible for the Status of Women
subsubtopic: COMPENSATION FOR PETER TREU-MINISTER'S POSITION
speechtext:
The matter of compensation in general is one which the Law Reform Commission is studying at the present time and upon which it will report. Also, I must remind the hon. member that the provinces will have to be involved very closely with this, because they would be the ones to bear most of the burden of such a situation if such a decision was reached, that compensation should be established as a practice. Thus, that is the general principle.
As far as this particular case is concerned, as I indicated to the hon. member, I have reviewed this case very carefully. I have come to the conclusion, without any doubt, that the charge made against Dr. Treu was not a frivolous one. He was charged with a very serious offence. There was a preliminary inquiry in which a prima facie case was found which allowed
Oral Questions
the case to be taken to trial. There was a trial before a judge at which Dr. Treu was convicted of the offence, and then it went to appeal where he was acquitted. As far as I am concerned, that man has been acquitted by the courts at the appeal level and he should be recognized as innocent; but I do not think in those circumstances there is any basis for compensation.

subsubtopic: COMPENSATION FOR PETER TREU-MINISTER'S POSITION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this charge followed only after a 1 '/2-year investigation which proved to be fruitless and cost the government several hundred thousand dollars. Last summer, when this case was at its height, there was an attempt by suggestion and innuendo to prevent members of the press and even myself from pursuing it. There were elements of the government at different levels which hinted that there was much more involved in this case and, "If Baldwin only knew, he would shut up."
Forgetting the question of justice, and on the question of equity from a government which once professed to believe in a just society, does the government not feel this man merits some recognition?

subsubtopic: CANADA'S ROLE IN UN NEGOTIATIONS ON CHINA-VIETNAM CONFLICT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my question is directed to the Secretary of State for External Affairs and concerns Canada's role in the negotiations going on today at the United Nations to end the China-Vietnam conflict.
Is it the view of the government that a compromise resolution is possible and acceptable to the three veto powers and, if so, is Canada co-ordinating this approach to the negotiations with other countries, particularly our NATO allies?

speakeroldname: Hon. Donald C. Jamieson (Secretary of State for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subsubtopic: CANADA'S ROLE IN UN NEGOTIATIONS ON CHINA-VIETNAM CONFLICT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the question is to some extent hypothetical because, I suppose, the answer would depend in large measure upon the particular wording of the resolution. I can only tell the hon. member that the resolution presented before the Security Council is apparently not acceptable to at least the Soviet Union, which has already indicated that it intends to vote against it or to veto it, whichever is the most appropriate method.
As to co-ordination, we have been in consultation with various other parties. We are not now a member of the Security Council, but we have been in discussion with other parties at the UN. I think our position was made very clear in a quite excellent statement by Ambassador Barton which no doubt the hon. member has seen.

subsubtopic: CANADA'S ROLE IN UN NEGOTIATIONS ON CHINA-VIETNAM CONFLICT
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, the U.S.S.R. keeps warning or suggesting that Peking should withdraw "before it is too late". Given the Soviet military activity in the Southeast theatre today, has the Government of Canada expressed its concern to Moscow or suggested that Soviet rhetoric and activity ought to be reduced in order to give the rest of the world an opportunity to find a proper and acceptable solution to this conflict?

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subsubtopic: CANADA'S ROLE IN UN NEGOTIATIONS ON CHINA-VIETNAM CONFLICT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I indicated six or seven days ago that we had, in fact, made representations not by way of

note but by way of personal intervention, on my instruction, to our ambassadors to Moscow and Peking and also indirectly to the Cambodians and Vietnamese that we feel that the four parties-certainly three of them, anyway-the Russians, the Chinese and the Vietnamese, ought to withdraw from their various incursions and, in the case of the Soviet Union, which has not made incursions, that it ought to be temperate in its remarks.
We indicated that, indeed, the only solution possible in our view-a view I am sure is shared by all members-is in the form of talks and negotiations taking place, and that it would be advisable that all parties withdraw their forces from those various places in an effort to get these kind of talks under way.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my question for the President of the Treasury Board is based on government statistics that came out just today, showing another form of gross discrimination against women in the public service.
In view of the fact that, for example, in the professional and scientific category 23 per cent of the employees are women, the other 77 per cent being men, but with recent lay-offs under the restraint program 56 per cent of the lay-offs have been women with the other 44 per cent being men, what steps does the President of the Treasury Board propose to take, in view of the declared policy that the government is in favour of women's rights, in order to reverse this trend and to make sure at least that it does not continue to happen?

speakeroldname: Hon. Judd Buchanan (President of the Treasury Board):
speakerposition: President of the Treasury Board
subsubtopic: LAY-OFFS UNDER RESTRAINT PROGRAM-ALLEGED DISCRIMINATION AGAINST WOMEN

Mr. Speaker, the hon. member is correct in pointing this out. It is a fact that occurs. 1 was particularly encouraged to note that when you break them down into the senior, intermediate and junior levels for the scientific catefory, the administrative and foreign service, we have been making significant headway, particularly-and I think this is encouraging-at the junior levels. February 27, 1979

greater than that of their percentage of the work force. That being the case, surely there is a need for some correction.

speakerposition: President of the Treasury Board
subsubtopic: LAY-OFFS UNDER RESTRAINT PROGRAM-ALLEGED DISCRIMINATION AGAINST WOMEN

We have moved up from a little over 31 per cent to about 35 per cent women in the public service. I think we are moving by trend and direction in the right way. subsubtopic: LAY-OFFS UNDER RESTRAINT PROGRAM-ALLEGED DISCRIMINATION AGAINST WOMEN

subsubtopic: APPLICATION OF CANADIAN HUMAN RIGHTS ACT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I want to put a question to the Minister of Justice relating to questions that were asked a few moments ago about the Canadian Human Rights Commission and the opinion expressed by the commissioner.
Could the minister tell the House whether it is now the policy of the government to distinguish between the statutes and agencies to which the Canadian Human Rights Act applies? I have in mind Bill C-22, wherein clause 7.1 reads:
Nothing in this act shall be construed as limiting the application of the Canadian Human Rights Act.
The government has laid that out. The Canadian Human Rights Act, section 63.1, reads as follows:
This act is binding on Her Majesty in right of Canada-
It would seem that these sections are precisely the same, in effect, in law.
Is it now the position of the government that it will choose when the Canadian Human Rights Act will not apply; that it will apply when it is convenient but it will not apply when it is inconvenient to the government?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada; Minister responsible for the Status of Women
subsubtopic: APPLICATION OF CANADIAN HUMAN RIGHTS ACT
speechtext:
Of course not, Mr. Speaker. The role of the government is to try to apply the law, but when there is a genuine doubt or apparent conflict between statutes the normal course is to ask for an interpretation by the courts. If the courts find that there is no contradiction, there would be no problem, but if there is a problem then the task would be to clarify the law; to come in the normal way before parliament to get the law clarified.
I think the best interpreters of the law are still the courts of this land. I am surprised that the hon. member would raise objections to going before the courts to get clarification of the law as soon as possible so that the intention of parliament can be made quite clear. If it needs to be clarified any further, then we can come back with further amendments to the law.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
subsubtopic: APPLICATION OF CANADIAN HUMAN RIGHTS ACT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I think the Minister of Justice is suffering from a conflict of interest between his position as Minister of Justice, on the one hand,

February 27, 1979

I put this question to him now as Attorney General of Canada. Given the fact that the Canadian Human Rights Act says, "This act is binding on Her Majesty", and given the fact that the Canadian Human Rights Act also says that the purpose of the act is to extend the present laws of Canada to the purview of matters coming within the legislative authority of the Parliament of Canada-which certainly covers immigration-will the minister ask the House for consent to table those documents which he says the rules of the House make it impossible or improper for him to table? I can give an undertaking that we on this side of the House are prepared to give our consent.
Will the minister take advantage of this, in his capacity as Attorney General, and table the documents so that not only will the courts be apprised some day with respect to its position but this parliament, which passed a law believing it was of universal application, will have a chance to look at it as well? Will he do that?

speakeroldname: Hon. Bud Cullen (Minister of Employment and Immigration):

speakerposition: Minister of Employment and Immigration

subsubtopic: MR. WOOLLIAMS-STATEMENT OF MINISTER OF JUSTICE CONCERNING PETER TREU CASE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise on a question of privilege. The Minister of Justice (Mr. Lalonde) in answering the distinguished member for Peace River (Mr. Baldwin) in reference to the Treu case, used the term as an excuse for non-payment of compensation that a prima facie case had been made out in the preliminary hearing. The Minister of Justice has said on another occasion today that he does not quote the law. I would like to give the Minister of Justice a chance to correct this statement because the Saskatchewan Court of Appeal said this in dealing with what is necessary in a preliminary hearing:
For committal for trial the Crown merely has to show that the accused is probably guilty and there is sufficient evidence ... in favour of the Crown.
It is a matter of sufficiency. That has been upheld by the Supreme Court of Canada in the following words:
The "justice", in accordance with this principle, is, in my opinion, required to commit an accused person for trial in any case in which there is admissible evidence which could, if it were believed, result in a conviction.
My point is that in a preliminary hearing a prima facie case does not have to be made out. It is a question of sufficiency of
Privilege-Mr. Abbott
evidence and if believed-if it could be believed by a judge and jury or a judge alone-then that person could be sent up for trial. The Minister of Justice left the impression that there was a prima facie case made out against Mr. Treu. That is an error in law and an error in fact.

It is an initiative of the federal government and the general plan for the area is being prepared by the Ministry of State for Urban Affairs in conjunction with other federal departments and the other levels of government. The study area is 450 acres (180 ha).

The MSUA research and demonstration group are responsible for the planning in co-operation with CMHC, Parks Canada, Public Works, NHB, and the provincial, MUC and city governments. The ultimate responsibility for carrying out specific projects within the over-all development plan will be determined as part of the planning process. The only monies spent to date have involved:
demolition of an unused grain elevator and dismantling the unused autostade by CMHC ($1.15 million), and
the opening of a project office and the beginning of planning by MSUA, $1.35 million.
acquisition of properties on St. Pierre Street to be renovated as housing by CMHC, $0.94 million.

It involves an association of interested individuals and groups with public meetings and workshops, as well as questionnaires and the solicitation of briefs and public suggestions. The civic groups who have so far chosen to become actively involved are: Association des locataires de Habitat 67, Association des proprietaires du vieux Montreal, Chambre de commerce du district de Montreal, Comite quebecois des sentiers de randonnee, Guilde de la marine marchande, Jeune Chambre de Montreal, Monde a bicyclette, Sauvons Montreal, STOP, Societe pour vaincre la pollution, Syndicat des initiatives du vieux Montreal.

(a)	Conserve and promote the Canadian cultural heritage.
(b)	Improve urban living conditions and facilitate public access to the water's edge within the constraints created by the presence of the harbour.
(c)	Contribute to the efforts for an economic recovery.
(d)	Maintain certain harbour functions that are congruous with the urban and historic environment.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-NON-CONFIDENCE MOTION- REQUESTED ESTABLISHMENT OF FAIR PRICES COMMISSION
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, the debate we are going to have this afternoon is one of the most important in the history of this parliament.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-NON-CONFIDENCE MOTION- REQUESTED ESTABLISHMENT OF FAIR PRICES COMMISSION
speechtext: Oh, oh!

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-NON-CONFIDENCE MOTION- REQUESTED ESTABLISHMENT OF FAIR PRICES COMMISSION
speechtext:
A Conservative member laughs. I hope he is as concerned about prices as most Canadians. I say it is one of the most important because the subject matter affects every Canadian. It affects pensioners, married couples, single people, trade unionists and non-trade unionists. The reality is that at this point in 1979 we are facing the clear prospect of a major new inflationary cycle.
The Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) has expressly said that he has not called an election because the Parliament of Canada has things to do. I cannot think of a subject matter that the people of this country would like parliament to deal with more than prices. If the Prime Minister is going to continue to hold off having an election on the ground that

parliament has things to do, I would like to see soon on the order paper a measure from the government, even just one, indicating that it wants to come to grips with this very serious matter.
In 1978 prices went up by some 9 per cent. The most recent figures show that that 9 per cent figure is continuing in 1979 and is in fact likely to worsen. That is on the price side. If you look at wages and salaries, the pay of Canadians, what do you find? Figures released on the weekend by Statistics Canada show that the average weekly earnings of Canadians increased from $252 a week to $269, an increase of only 6.4 per cent.
If you subtract the increase in the cost of living for 1978 from the increase in earnings, what do you find? I am sure even members of the cabinet can understand this reality. In 1978, the average Canadian worker had a net loss in his income of $340. His standard of living did not increase at all in
1978.	With price increases exceeding salary increases, the ordinary family is falling behind in an economic sense.
I am not so much concerned with 1978 as I am with what is going on right now in terms of what is in store for the rest of
1979.	Looking at the trends for the last quarter of 1978, the alarming conclusion one has to reach is that the net loss of income which became apparent in 1978 will be even worse for Canadian workers in 1979 unless something is done. The reality is that real incomes are falling behind.
Wage settlements continue to fall behind the increase in the cost of living. I learned of one settlement over the weekend affecting 18,000 hospital workers in Ontario. Hospital workers in every province are among the most poorly paid Canadians. Their settlement amounted to 4 per cent, or even slightly less. It does not take an economic genius to realise what is happening; even without briefing notes the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs (Mr. Allmand) could calculate that an increase of 4 per cent set against an increase in the cost of living conservatively estimated at 9 per cent for this year means a significant loss of income for those hospital workers. The fact is that thousands of workers who have been subjected to a wage control program for the past three years are now accepting similar settlements. It is time a measure of economic justice went in the direction of the workers. That is what this debate is all about.
The AIB report which came out over the weekend showed that food prices went up by some 21 per cent in the past year. Again, I should like the cabinet minister who will be replying in this debate on behalf of the government to consider the impact of this increase on a typical family. It is not so serious in its impact on members of parliament because compared with most Canadians we are well paid. It is not so serious in its impact on a civil servant who has just got a $5,000 increase in pay. But it is very serious for pensioners and low income earners who spend a much larger proportion of their incomes on food than do the rest of us. The price of hamburger meat, I heard not long ago, had reached $2 a pound and I am told it is now in excess of $2. A head of cauliflower in Ottawa costs
February 27, 1979

$1.98. Last week, in the same store, the price was $1.49. Vegetable prices have risen so high that a Liberal senator, a member of that other august body which joins us from time to time in assessing legislation, thought we should remove vegetables from the consumer price index. That is the Liberal way of dealing with the high price of food-remove it from the statistical accounting system. I am sure the hon. senator does not speak for the government in that regard but I should like to hear what members of the cabinet intend to do about the high cost of vegetables as well as of other food.
Today a loaf of bread costs 69 cents or 70 cents. Every food item is costing more day after day, as housewives know-they do not need politicians to tell them. Lumber prices are going up as well as steel prices which affect so many consumer needs. Car prices are going up. Prices in every sector of the economy are increasing, not declining. I asked my research staff to try to find evidence of some falling off in prices somewhere because it seemed to me that if we were getting increased efficiency as a basis for increases in profits some falling off in prices could be expected. But I am told there are no such reductions in prices. In the old days firms cut the prices of some of their products in order to win a larger share of the market; but nowadays prices are not reduced, they are set and then they are kept up.
So we are confronted by this reality. On one hand, wages and salaries have been controlled by the AIB for three years; controls have now been removed and there is every indication that the demands being made by workers are reasonable. On the other hand, prices and profits are going out of sight and it is obvious that something has to be done.
Something has to be done in terms of fairness for its own sake. What I want to emphasize today, however, is this. If we are to head off a new round of inflation in 1979, we must take action today for the Canadian worker on the price side of the ledger. If we expect men and women who will be coming to the bargaining table in 1979 to do what they normally do, which is to make reasonable wage demands, then we have to confront them with a reasonable price situation. As sure as we are sitting in this chamber today, Mr. Speaker, if the price escalation continues at its present rate, continues to rise in 1979 as it did in 1978, Canadian men and women who are bargaining for wages to ensure that their families have a reasonable existence will demand increases later this year which are at least equivalent to the increase in the cost of living. So the more the cost of living goes up, the more we can expect wage and salary demands to go up. And that is just, Mr. Speaker.
If you look at the period from 1945 to the present time you will find almost without exception, not only in this country but in the United States as well, wage and salary demands have invariably followed price increases, not the other way around. I read a report in the New York Times on Sunday which made the same case as I am making here.
The inflation we are now experiencing certainly has nothing to do with wage and salary demands. It has everything to do
Unfair Price Increases
with demands on the economy by the other side of the ledger. So what can we do? What has been the response of the government? The government, led by the Prime Minister, who says he does not want an election because parliament should be doing something, has not done a thing about increasing prices. In general, it has made three responses to questions my colleagues and I have been putting since Christmas in the House about price increases. On the one hand, when the government could get away with it, it has said that price increases are not real, that they do not exist and that we are making things up. That has happened from time to time. The Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs typifies that by his mobilized inaction. The typical response has been to say that the situation will be studied but that there is nothing the government can do. That has been the twofold response of the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs. The response has been to set up another study and to say in advance that there is nothing the government can do-and I am waiting to hear a report on at least one of these studies-even if the study concludes that there is price gouging.
There has not been one rollback ordered by this government, which is crucial if we are addressing our concern to the typical worker in Canada. Not one price has come down as a result of action by this government. Quite the contrary, by lifting subsidies recently on bread and milk and by allowing oil companies to get what they could in the market, this government has been directly responsible for many of the price increases which have taken place. I say on behalf of my colleagues that something can be done, and something must be done.
Before I indicate what must be done, I want to mention half a dozen examples because I think one example is worth a thousand generalizations. The people who are out there in the country certainly deal with concrete examples. They do not deal with annual figures put out by Statistics Canada, and I hope when the minister speaks on behalf of the government today he will deal with these cases because they point very clearly in one direction. This has caused me to conclude that we have to propose to this government a specific method for dealing with prices because the government has not been able to come up with one on its own.
First I want to deal with the general question of food prices. We know the government's response in this regard. Its response is that the low level of the Canadian dollar has meant that food prices are inescapably higher. Let me concede right off the bat that that is true in many cases. If we import orange juice or vegetables from Florida or California and our dollar is low, prices will be higher. Anyone who is honest must acknowledge that reality.
However, there is another reality about which the government does not like to talk, and I want to draw attention to it. The report issued by the AIB last week indicated that food store profits jumped 37.9 per cent in the third quarter of last year over the third quarter of 1977. In the same period-and this is the issue which concerns me-sales increased by only 17.4 per cent. In terms of elementary arithmetic, profits

February 27, 1979
Unfair Price Increases
increased at twice the rate of sales. We want to know the reason for that. It may be that there has been some remarkable new efficiency introduced by the food chains. It may be that there have been some devices or managerial actions which have led to profit increases twice that of sales. Perhaps some creative genius has been at work at the middle man level in the food sector.
If that is the case, I think Canadian consumers would like to know about it. All I am saying is that on the basis of past performance and trends there is good reason for us to conclude that food prices are too high because profits in large measure are too high in this sector, and that consumers are being charged much more than they ought to be charged. We say we would like that to be investigated. We would like to have some answers. I want to stress that we are not assuming that conclusion, but at least we have the honesty to look at the evidence and not just to ignore it.
Another example is flour. A five pound bag of Five Roses flour increased in price by some 44 cents from the first week in December to the middle of this month. A five pound bag is a relatively small amount, and it is very interesting that its price should increase 44 cents in a two-month period. The federal subsidy which had been on until the middle of December, when it was removed, was only 22 cents per five pound bag of flour, and the consumer was charged twice the amount he should have been charged if the removal of the subsidy were simply passed directly on. We say that that bears investigation. Why is the removal of the subsidy being compounded in its impact on the consumer?
Bread prices are seriously affected by the removal of that subsidy. We felt that subsidy should have been left on, and we urged that because bread is a basic food for Canadians. However, the government removed the subsidy. That ought to have increased the price of a loaf of bread three cents to four cents. Instead, the price went up between eight cents and ten cents. Now a family spends 69 cents or 70 cents when it buys a loaf of bread.
Then there is chicken. In view of the performance of the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs yesterday one is tempted to say that the chickens have come home to roost in terms of the government's lack of policy on consumer items. What is the reality regarding chicken prices? The AIB reported recently that poultry prices increased by some 33.5 per cent during the past year. However, the farmer got only 12.5 per cent of that. I think a legitimate question again arises: Where did the rest go? We are paying all that money for chickens; where did the rest go? The farmer does not have it.
The Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs does not like what he calls obscure questions. I find it difficult to understand why he regards questions about chicken prices and flour prices as obscure. However, that is his problem, not mine. The minister said in the House yesterday that the price of chicken went up because there was an increase in demand. Anyone who looks at the real world of economics knows that increase in demand is related to the question of supply and price. At one point in yesterday's question period the Minister

of Consumer and Corporate Affairs said to me that if I really understood reality I would know that when demand is increased prices go up.
Some 20 minutes later the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Whelan) let the truth be known when he revealed that during the past year the amount of frozen chicken increased. We have some four million more pounds of poultry frozen in storage- taken off the market-in 1979 than we had in 1978. That is the reason for the increase in price. Farmers have done their job, as they have traditionally done in Canada. One of the most efficient agricultural sectors of any country in the world exists in this country. Farmers have produced the chickens, but somehow the middle men have managed to take them off the market. They have kept four million pounds more in frozen storage instead of putting them on the market so that the Canadian consumer could pay a reasonable price. That is the real reason chicken prices have increased in response to demand.
With regard to lumber prices, there has been a 70 per cent increase in lumber prices over the past two years, with a further 10 per cent increase last month. This has added about $1,200, in terms of its economic impact on the economy, to the construction cost of a single family home with 1,800 square feet of floor space. One board foot of two-by-four spruce now retails at 23 cents, compared to 17 cents last year. Plywood prices are up to $14.25 from $11 for a four-by-eight foot sheet of half inch spruce sheeting. The big six of the pulp and paper industry, the companies which have benefited so recently from another multi-million dollar handout from this government, have recorded a 123 per cent increase in profits, from $182 million in 1977 to $407 million in 1978. I suggest that perhaps there is some exaggeration in the profit there, that perhaps there is some slight overcharging to the consumer. I suggest that if the government is interested in heading off potentially inflationary demands coming on the wage and salary side in 1979, lumber prices, among others, are areas in which the government should be zeroing in and, more than that, areas in which they should be turning around those price increases.
What about the poor banks? The major banks in Canada, that handful of financial entities protected by government legislation from outside competition, that small group of Canadian banks, had almost a $1 billion net profit last year. They in turn are increasing charges now for everyone-farmers, small businessmen, everyone who has an account-for the services they get. At the same time their profits are going right out of sight.
Finally, I will turn to the farmer. What about his input costs? Right now, a 100 horsepower tractor sells for some $28,000, up 16 per cent over last year. A combine, which is rather essential for our farmers in western Canada in particular but by no means exclusively there, went up in price in the past year from $32,000 to over $41,000, up some 30 per cent in one year. I stress again that this has come about precisely at a time when wage and salary increases were going up slightly
February 27, 1979

in excess of 6 per cent. In this case it is not the worker who is getting more than his share; it is someone else who has come between the industrial worker and the farmer. It is someone else who is getting that 30 per cent rip-off.
Therefore, it seems to me that farm input costs have to be considered rather seriously, and I say that particularly in the context of 1979 when the federal Department of Agriculture forecast that net farm income in 1979 will go down compared to 1978, not up.
Very clearly, something has to be done. I have given a number of examples. I could without any difficulty have given a dozen more examples which would require any fair-minded person or any fair-minded government to take action.
What are we recommending? We are saying that the pressures on the economy at this time very clearly are not on the wage and salary side; very clearly they are on the price side from sources other than wages and salaries. Very clearly they are up and going higher. Both in terms of present justice to the consumer and in terms of having a favourable impact on wage and salary settlements in 1979 further down the road, something must be done now about prices.
Therefore, we are proposing-so that the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs will not have to rise day after day to say that the government has no authority to do this- the establishment of a fair prices commission. We say that the commission should have the following powers. First, on a selective basis, it should investigate prima facie unfair prices for food, essential household services, basic industrial commodities and farm input costs.
Second, it should have the power to delay price increases while these investigations are under way.
Third, it should have the power to obtain full information from corporations in sectors in which it is investigating a particular price increase.
Fourth, it should have the power to order rollbacks when unfair prices are discovered.
In our view, this commission should consist simply of five or six members, with a staff seconded to it by other departments that are relevant to financial concerns. There is no need to create an elaborate bureaucracy.
The way we see this commission functioning is exactly analogous, in terms of federal government authority, to the kind of influence exercised in the U.S. economy in the past by presidents Kennedy and Johnson. In the past, both those U.S. presidents singled out the steel sector which, during their respective presidencies, was proposing unjustified price increases. They had the presidential authority and the moral authority that the leader in any country should have but that we have lacked in this country. Those two presidents took on the steel industry and said that their price increases were unjustified and should be stopped. This had a significant impact on prices throughout the economy because other firms were made aware of the fact that the government meant business.
Unfair Price Increases
This is precisely the purpose of this commission. We see it functioning on a selective basis and zeroing in on particular targets, taking particular examples and, when it finds unfair price increases ordering rollbacks. With that kind of action we do not think it at all necessary to have across the board controls. Not only are they cumbersome and unworkable, as we have seen they are unnecessary. That is the point I am making. A selective approach at this time could have major effect because, when it rolls back a few prices, all those in the economy who had the temptation in the same year to levy unwarranted prices will not do so. That is what we think should be the effect. We think that action is overdue. We think this fair prices commission, which by no means would guarantee perfectly just prices to Canadians, would at least provide them with something they have lacked for a long time, and that is fair prices.

speakeroldname: Hon. Robert K. Andras (President of the Board of Economic Development Ministers):
speakerposition: Minister of State for Economic Development
subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-NON-CONFIDENCE MOTION- REQUESTED ESTABLISHMENT OF FAIR PRICES COMMISSION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I welcome this debate today on the subject of inflation, a matter of deserved concern to all of us, and certainly a matter of overriding concern to the government. Our policies have been directed for quite some time toward trying to alleviate and bring inflation under control while avoiding other kinds of adjustments across the economy. It is always a finely balanced and difficult action to take.
I will not pretend today that we have succeeded totally in meeting our goal of reducing the rate of inflation, but I think there is good evidence, if people want to examine objectively the record, that we are on the road to a better price performance and that we are doing better in that area than most other industrialized nations. There have been some setbacks on the road, there is no question about it. They come mainly as the result of elements beyond our domestic control. But even here we are trying to meet and overcome them. We have a long haul ahead, as does every country that we can examine, but I think I want to stress the need in this country, and I think the justification, for having confidence.
1 believe there is a mounting sense of optimism that I detect in our economy, perhaps not among members on the benches opposite or among some of the theoretical economists. Let us look for a few minutes at what has been happening on the inflation front. It was approximately five years ago that Canada was hit, as other countries were hit, by the shock of double-digit inflation with price increases in 1974 and 1975 touching close to the 11 per cent mark. That situation forced introduction of the anti-inflation program in the fall of 1975 and the imposition of anti-inflation controls which helped to bring down prices and to bring about a gradual turnaround in the price situation. But I think we all realize that a control program of that nature is a psychological weapon in the main and is consistent only with the market economy if it is in place for a limited period of time. Thus, the process of decontrol was put in motion approximately a year ago, in April of last year.

February 27, 1979
Unfair Price Increases
During that same month in his spring budget, the Minister of Finance (Mr. Chretien) said that the increase in the consumer price index during 1978, in his opinion, would be approximately 7 per cent. It turned out to be 9 per cent, in the main because of unexpectedly high food prices and a further devaluation of the dollar, the other side of that coin, which pushed up the cost of all goods which we import.
Given no surprises, this year we expect the CPI to rise between 7 per cent and 7.5 per cent, but again food and imports will be the main contributors to that price increase. I am not saying for a moment the size of that increase is acceptable to us, but it will be significantly below the rates experienced in the past few years.
The motion before the House in the name of the hon. leader of the New Democratic Party purports to be a solution to the increased burden which inflation places on Canadian families. It would create a new agency which would apparently oversee pricing practices in this country, but in our view it does not address the basic problem. Indeed it would be irrelevant to many of the most important sources of current price increases. In addition it deals only with prices and ignores the basic cost elements, which are the essential foundations of the price structure, as though they do not exist. Time and time again it has been proven in this country and elsewhere that prices cannot be controlled in isolation from costs, wages, profits and dividends.
I imagine the hon. leader of the New Democratic Party would expect the agency to go to work first in the areas where prices are rising fastest, some of which he pointed out today. After all, when one is hunting elephants it is wise to go into elephant country. I suspect the hon. member would want that agency to look at food prices first, particularly beef, which are the main concerns of Canadian shoppers today. Although the leader of the New Democratic Party carefully avoided this, I wonder if he is prepared also to confront the cattleman and tell him that his prices are too high.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-NON-CONFIDENCE MOTION- REQUESTED ESTABLISHMENT OF FAIR PRICES COMMISSION
speechtext: The answer is no.

speakerposition: Minister of State for Economic Development
subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-NON-CONFIDENCE MOTION- REQUESTED ESTABLISHMENT OF FAIR PRICES COMMISSION
speechtext:
After suffering through several years of depressed prices and rising costs, I can imagine the response the hon. member would get from the cattle farmer. Thus, the hon. member wants to cut in at some other level. He has been critical of the food processing industry over the last several weeks, but conveniently ignored the extensive investigation of the food processing and food retailing industry which was carried out just a few months ago by the Anti-Inflation Board and updated last week on the basis of third quarter data. The study concluded that profit margins in the industry varied very little from historic norms during the first nine months of 1978.
The AIB found that the profit margin was increasing, but it found that the profit margin was 3.3 per cent in food processing which was identical to the same period in 1977. In the food wholesaling area, profit margins moved up slightly from 1.21 per cent to 1.30 per cent in the periods under comparison. For

food retailers, the profit margin was 1.88 per cent in the 1978 period and 1.80 per cent in 1977. Profit margins in the beverage industry declined between 1971 and 1978.
Perhaps the New Democratic Party through this agency would be prepared to tackle the number two villain on the price scene-imports. Approximately 30 per cent of the goods consumed by the Canadians come from outside the country. Foreign producers are facing price increases of their own, and the devaluation of the Canadian dollar against foreign currencies means that it costs us more to import foreign products.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-NON-CONFIDENCE MOTION- REQUESTED ESTABLISHMENT OF FAIR PRICES COMMISSION
speechtext: Right.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-NON-CONFIDENCE MOTION- REQUESTED ESTABLISHMENT OF FAIR PRICES COMMISSION
speechtext: I do not know whether the NDP is suggesting that this agency would roll back the prices paid to California lettuce producers or Florida orange growers.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-NON-CONFIDENCE MOTION- REQUESTED ESTABLISHMENT OF FAIR PRICES COMMISSION
speechtext: Did the minister listen to my speech? I said no.

speakerposition: Minister of State for Economic Development
subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-NON-CONFIDENCE MOTION- REQUESTED ESTABLISHMENT OF FAIR PRICES COMMISSION
speechtext:
The hon. member has one precise point at which he cuts in, and the entire sequence of the food chain, food pricing and its mechanics seem to be a mystery to him. In any event, the hon. member thinks this is a magic wand he can wave and our exchange rate problems will disappear and all those factors will be settled.
I should like to remind members of the House that in the spring of 1974 the government presented a bill to parliament. It was an amendment to the Combines Investigation Act which would have enabled the government temporarily to freeze prices on goods where there was evidence of profiteering and to roll back prices in those circumstances. When the then minister of consumer and corporate affairs introduced the bill he said that it was designed to "stop business from taking advantage of current economic conditions to unduly enhance profits." The bill was opposed by the same opposition critics who sit across the floor today. It died on the order paper when parliament was dissolved for the general election of 1974. Following the election, the government re-examined the whole question of prices, particularly food prices, and decided that the bill introduced previously was no longer effective in the changing economic situation.

speechtext:
From that study we developed the concept of the anti-inflation program which was put in place in the fall of 1975. That policy on prices included guidelines which limited price increases to the recovery of added costs. Profits were restricted to margins no higher than 95 per cent of a firm's pre-tax net profit margin in the average of the previous five years. That policy worked well during the period of the anti-inflation program.
At the end of the controls it was decided at a conference of first ministers to ask the Economic Council of Canada to continue an analysis of price and cost developments. That request led to the establishment of the Centre for the Study of Inflation and Productivity. That agency was assigned the task
February 27, 1979

of monitoring prices and incomes to inform the public of developments which appear to threaten our ability to reduce inflation. As well it was instructed to investigate structural problems which may add to costs or prices and leave the economy more vulnerable to inflationary shocks. Just recently the executive of CSIP wrote to the major corporations for additional information on costs and prices to expand its work of analysis.
That is the extent of its mandate, but I should like to point out that the original proposal put forward by the federal government to the premiers of the provinces at the time of the federal-provincial conference in February, 1978, was a stronger agency with greater powers, not roll-back powers but greater investigative and mandatory powers to demand information and so on. Frankly, it was the provincial premiers who resisted that and asked us not to go ahead. The premier of New Brunswick said that he would support a lesser powered agency. He suggested in reviewing the changes which have been made in it that we should stop calling it a monitoring agency because it implies a certain amount of compulsion. He said he would like to see this set up and have it operate on a voluntary basis. That is the view of New Brunswick.
Mr. Davis of Ontario had great reservations about having this-

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-NON-CONFIDENCE MOTION- REQUESTED ESTABLISHMENT OF FAIR PRICES COMMISSION
speechtext: Leave it to the provinces again.

speakerposition: Minister of State for Economic Development
subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-NON-CONFIDENCE MOTION- REQUESTED ESTABLISHMENT OF FAIR PRICES COMMISSION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, there is going to be a very interesting bit of information in a minute. Mr. Davis said that what he is looking for is to get out of involvement as government and, as much as we can, allow the business community and the collective bargaining process to function in its normal fashion. He said there should be a very clear understanding that this is a transitory sort of thing and that we are not just moving from one phase of controls to another for an unstated period of time.
I have a more definite, more positive and more precise description of concern expressed by one premier, Premier Blakeney of Saskatchewan. He clearly said that he wanted to make a very precise comment. He said that in its present form, the stronger form that was presented by the federal government to that conference, they oppose the monitoring agency, and they have no doubts about that at all. He suggested that we are in a world of psychology, and it seemed to him that if we are to foster an economic recovery we need the psychological benefit of a definite end to control, a clean break and not any haphazard return to a food prices review board. He went on to say that he really thought what we needed, in his judgment, was a clean break so that everybody will know that the control program is over and that we are all back into the business of setting prices and incomes by the market forces.
The premier of Saskatchewan went on to indicate his clear opinion that it seemed to him we have to face up to the fact that we will have to establish prices and incomes by market forces sooner or later, and it may as well be sooner. He did not
Unfair Price Increases
think putting off the inevitable would do anything except prolong the confusion.
There is dissension. The provinces do not want us to proceed with a stronger agency than the present Centre for the Study of Inflation and Productivity. I want to indicate that the Minister of Finance, along with the cabinet, is seriously looking at the centre, and there is serious consideration as to whether there are additional monitoring powers that may or may not be necessary clearly to establish before the Canadian people whether there is profiteering. Whatever is decided on, it will fall definitely short of rollback. We do not intend to go that route. There are many reasons why we feel that would be the wrong thing to do. In the end the real key to controlling inflation is a strong and a growing economy functioning under responsible monetary and fiscal policies. That has to be the basis for full recovery and expansion in the private sector.
We took the decision a few years ago, along with the provinces, to begin to control our spending, holding it below the rate of growth in the GNP, and this is being accomplished. Monetary policy is reflecting our concern about inflation. There are a great number of other strong influences at work stimulating private sector activity. Our improvement in the international competitive situation is capable of documentation. Our domestic costs have come down at a time when the external value of the Canadian dollar has declined. We have seen a dramatic gain in jobs, more than 440,000 in the past 12 months, and we have seen a record $3.5 billion surplus in merchandise trade for 1978. Manufacturing has been recovering strongly over the past year with output up by 9 per cent and employment up by 7 per cent. We are confident that real growth this year will be about 3.5 per cent, and investment intentions which are already known suggest there will be growth in real investment of 4 per cent to 5 per cent for the economy as a whole.
The word "profit" was mentioned. I think it is a very important aspect of the recovery that this country has seen in economic terms that profits are improving. People can play games with percentage increases. One dollar profit this year on a million dollar investment is not very much. You can double that to $2 profit next year and you have a 100 per cent increase. You really have to dig a lot deeper than the leader of the NDP is digging to indicate a true pattern there.
Quite frankly, profit is not a dirty word to me. It is the main source of the capital investment that we need to produce jobs, protect jobs and create the growth this country really needs. It is something that should be welcomed by every sector of the economy, by labour as well as business, because without profits the money available for labour for decent wages and for the protection of jobs is simply not there.
We think the pieces are in place for sound expansion of the economy. We are admittedly concerned about the surge in imported food prices which is squeezing the real income of workers. We do not deny that, or that this is making the transition to lower inflation that much more difficult. But it is a serious question as to whether we can protect the people of this country from all aspects of imported inflation. Most

February 27, 1979
Unfair Price Increases
certainly any over-zealous attempt to interfere with the workings of the marketplace, where there is no evidence of a scapegoat, as there is not in respect of food prices, could be a response in the wrong direction. We could respond the wrong way and turn back the progress which has been so painfully established over the past few years.
Finally, there are real and technical difficulties with regard to the hon. member's proposal for a rollback. I think he is well aware of the constitutional position and that the federal government would have no such powers, except perhaps in a few areas of federal jurisdiction, such as the banks which he suggested. In the rest, a rollback power legislated by us would have to take place only on the basis of an emergency, as the anti-inflation program itself. It is very, very doubtful whether that could be proven is a case of law, and it is very doubtful in my mind whether that degree of urgency does in fact exist.
I have indicated the reaction of provincial governments. I have indicated the reaction of the government of Saskatchewan, which was most forceful of all, surprisingly, in saying it is time to let the market forces work. We are not about to embark on an agency with rollback provisions. We are not going into controls. We are coming out of those controls and it is somewhat painful. We are looking to the responsibility of the main actors in the marketplace to realize that we cannot, all or any of us, take more out of this economy than we are prepared to put into it.
I sense a great deal of responsibility on the part of labour groups. I agree with the leader of the NDP and his comments in that regard because I have been talking to labour and I see a much greater degree of rapport between business and labour. I am just back from British Columbia where there was a very encouraging recognition of much better dialogue between the main forces in the economy there. I hope that spreads. I hope these profits which the leader of the NDP is so ashamed of do get ploughed back into plant expansion and into competitive modernization so they can stay competitive in international markets particularly and protect and expand job creation. To knock them and to denigrate profits, and to start opting for artificial interventions in the marketplace when the facts do not yet warrant it, is the fastest way to turn off this return to profits and job creation that we see taking place.
I repeat that we are looking very carefully at the activities of the agency now in place; the Minister of Finance is taking this very seriously indeed. I think he will have some comments to make within the next few days, but I assure you that these activities will not be expanded, nor will we include the power of rollback.

speakeroldname: Mr. Janies A. McGrath (St. John's East):
subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-NON-CONFIDENCE MOTION- REQUESTED ESTABLISHMENT OF FAIR PRICES COMMISSION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, what is significant about the speech that we just heard is the fact that it was made by the President of the Board of Economic Development Ministers (Mr. Andras) and not by the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs (Mr. All-mand). I would expect him to speak but my point is that I fully expected him to lead off this debate for the government since it

is he who has the statutory responsibility within government. I intend to come back to that in a few minutes, Mr. Speaker.
The motion put forward by the hon. member for Oshawa-Whitby (Mr. Broadbent) is simplistic and, on the surface, commendable. This kind of simplistic approach is quite typical of the New Democratic Party. They come up with what is a reasonably adequate diagnosis of the symptoms but then they provide a remedy that amounts to a band-aid. We do not want another band-aid, Mr. Speaker. What we want is a cure. What this country wants is a cure.
I hope that the Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance (Mr. Martin) who makes a positive contribution to this House from time to time, Mr. Speaker, will make one on his feet during the debate and not from his seat.
The President of the Board of Economic Development Ministers referred in his speech to the parliament of 1972-74 and the amendments to the Combines Investigation Act introduced at that time by the then minister of consumer and corporate affairs. Those amendments, of course, were to provide, where necessary, the kind of rollback power called for in the motion put forward by the hon. member for Oshawa-Whitby in setting up his fair prices commission.
Of course, as the minister indicated in his speech, the amendments died with the dissolution of that parliament when we had a general election. I look forward to hearing the hon. member for Halifax (Mr. Stanfield) in this regard, because what is interesting is that when the government came back with a renewed mandate, they did not introduce the amendments to the Combines Investigation Act, which would have been the decent, honest and consistent thing to do, but proceeded to introduce that which they had campaigned against, namely, wage and price controls.
We all remember that campaign and the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) going about the country saying "Zap, you are frozen", speaking against any kind of controls. And then when we came back he forgot about the previous parliament and the need to amend the Combines Investigation Act, competition policy and all the things that would have a meaningful effect in the marketplace. Instead we got a controls program.
I suppose that is all we can expect from this government but we are getting a little tired of hearing the government, in debate after debate, regardless of the issue, parading statements by provincial premiers and socking it to the provinces instead of hearing clear statements on where the government stands and what it proposes to do about the economic situation in the country today. We certainly did not get it from the President of BED Ministers as he attempted to speak for the government in replying to the hon. member for Oshawa-Whitby. We got from him, however, a hint that if this parliament lasts that long they are going to-I hesitate to use the word- "beef' up the Centre for the Study of Productivity and Inflation. What they propose to do about that toothless, useless agency whose credibility has already been destroyed is beyond me.
February 27, 1979

The problem in the first place was the failure to establish that agency under the aegis of the Inquiries Act which would give it the authority to act that it does not presently have. In consequence of some of the incorrect pronouncements it has spouted, it has lost whatever credibility it may have had as it sets out to monitor the marketplace. I suppose one can draw from the fact that the President of the Board of Economic Development Ministers spoke for the government, instead of the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs or the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Whelan), the conclusion that finally the government is beginning to get its act together with respect to some kind of strategy on prices. Perhaps the President of the Board of Economic Development Ministers is finally emerging as the minister who will be responsible for co-ordinating that food strategy we have heard so much about from the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs, the Minister of Agriculture and others.
Perhaps that is what the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs was referring to last week when he stated to the press what he has tried to correct or deny in the House, namely: "There is going to be a statement-something is happening. I cannot tell you very much but things are happening. We are going to have a statement on co-ordinated food strategy. All I can tell you is that I will not be making that statement, it will be some other minister."
It will not be the Minister of Agriculture; obviously he lost the battle too. That is how we can explain his absence from the House today. Obviously it is not going to be the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs. Perhaps the President of the Board of Economic Development Ministers will finally have something to co-ordinate. Let us hope that at last he will be able to bring it all together.
What do we mean when we speak of co-ordination in terms of food strategy, Mr. Speaker? We mean the co-ordination of various government departments that are the responsibility of divers government ministers. We mean somebody to co-ordinate the policies of the Minister of Agriculture on the one hand, who has a responsibility to the producers of this country, and the policies of the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs on the other hand, who has a very definite statutory responsibility to the consumers of this country.
Bringing up the rear is the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce (Mr. Horner) who has some say with respect to imports into the country. We are told that a large part of food inflation at the moment is represented by imports. Then there is the Minister of Transport (Mr. Lang) who controls the Canadian Wheat Board. He rises in his place in this House without regard to the consequences and in one fell swoop eliminates the consumer subsidy on domestically consumed wheat, notwithstanding the fact that this means a minimum 15 per cent increase in the price of a loaf of bread, an increase in the price of flour, some of which increase cannot be justified, an increase in the price of pasta products and all the things made from wheat.

Then we have the Minister of Fisheries and the Environment (Mr. LeBlanc) representing a major food ministry of this government.
I do not know what the hon. member from New Brunswick is trying to say from his seat, Mr. Speaker. I hope he says it on his feet before the debate is over.
The Minister of Fisheries and the Environment has a definite responsibility in this House. The price of fish is good. The price of fish is too high for the same reason that the price of beef is too high. This is because it is priced on the American market and because of our sinking dollar. That is the reason we have to pay so much for fish in Canada. I hope the hon. member would address himself to that question. But when one talks about the price of fish, it speaks to the fact that we, as one of the great and most important fishing nations of the world, have one of the smallest per capita consumptions of fish. I believe we consume somewhere between 13 pounds and 15 pounds of fish per capita per annum. Something that should be addressed by government policy is how we can increase the consumption of fish in Canada.
All of these things have to be brought together in some kind of a co-ordinated strategy. On the one hand the Minister of Agriculture talks about supply and management with the various marketing boards that are able to control supply. On the other hand we have the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce who has to react to whatever the Minister of Agriculture says every time there is a request to limit or increase the supply of chickens coming into the country. The same holds true for eggs and turkeys.
I want to make this very clear just in case it has not been made clear before. The last thing Canadians want is another commission. We are fed up with commissions. What we want is action. We want a government that is prepared to act. We do not want another bureaucracy. Look at what we have had. That is all we have had from this government. Now all we are getting from the NDP is this cry of "set up another commission; set up another agency." How many commissions and how many agencies have we had since 1968 when the Prime Minister promised or told us that he had wrestled inflation to the ground?
Let us look back and recall some of them. As I recall, we had the prices and incomes commission, of late and unlamented memory. This was a useless agency which put together a substantial and expensive bureaucracy only to be disbanded.
Then as a response to the politics of the food situation which was getting to be a hot political issue in 1972, the government opened parliament with a big announcement in the Speech from the Throne that it was concerned about food prices and the effect of rising food prices, and that it was going to do something about it. But what did the government do? It set up another commission. This was the special commission on trends in food prices. It is interesting to note that the Minister of Employment and Immigration (Mr. Cullen) was the distinguished chairman of that committee. He has since been resur-

That committee recommended, among other things, when it made its final report in 1973, a ten-year food strategy for Canada. That was in 1973, six years ago. Instead of having government action on food strategy for Canada, as recommended by an all party committee of this House, we had that special committee, the food prices review board under the guidance of Mrs. Plumptre. We are all in favour of fair prices. What I find rather interesting about this proposal put forward by the hon. member for Oshawa-Whitby is that, no matter how he tries to talk about it, it is just another form of controls, the very controls which day after day he has spoken against in this House. Now he intends to set up another controls mechanism. By listening to the hon. member's argument very carefully one could hear the hon. member arguing against his own proposal.
If we examine the experience of the Anti-Inflation Board- the controls program which is now supposed to be deactivated-what do we find? We find that in the first year of the setting up of the AIB the rate of inflation was 7.5 per cent. The reason it was 7.5 per cent had nothing to do with the controls program. During the first year of the Anti-Inflation Board there was a fairly substantial drop in food prices, which were not controlled in any case by the AIB at the time. Then in 1977 the rate of inflation rose to 8 per cent. Again in the final year of the controls program, 1978, the rate of inflation was at 9 per cent. At the rate we are going this year we are heading into double-digit inflation. All of this was happening at a time when the government's target for inflation at the time it set up the AIB was 4 per cent. We should now be at an annual rate of inflation of 4 per cent. That is not bad, Mr. Speaker. If you look at the figures, I estimate they are out about 125 per cent, which is not bad for this government given some of its other forecasts. The rate of inflation for the final year of the controls program was the third worst in our history and the second worst in the industrial world. Only Italy had a worse rate. Now we are going to have another controls mechanism.
I do not understand the hon. member for Oshawa-Whitby. He has identified what has happened. He identified that prices have gone ahead and wages are falling behind. He knows that during the last two years of the controls program wages fell behind by an average of $520.
It boggles the mind to understand how the hon. member can get up in this House and with a straight face put forward this kind of proposal which is not worth the paper on which it is written. I have heard members of the Tory party suggest that the currency situation today is dangerous and bad for the Canadian economy, and this at a time when the price of fish, lumber, wood products, peat moss and minerals makes the Canadian economy more competitive and gives us a better edge in penetrating markets, some of which we have lost over the years. I have heard Tories, including the hon. member for St. John's East, complain about that in the House. Fishermen and those who work in the woods and in the peat moss industry, when purchasing equipment such as outboard motors, chain saws, trucks or mill equipment, have to pay the North American or world price. However, the Tories suggest that fishermen or those in the lumber industry should not get the world price.
People who work in the resource industries have traditionally had lower salaries than those who work in central Canada or in secondary manufacturing. The philosophy of the Tories is that because we have a currency exchange situation which benefits those people because the industries in which they work can better penetrate the market and receive better prices, that is bad. I find it terrible that a Newfoundland member would suggest that kind of policy.
A week or ten days ago the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Clark) said that he generally agreed with the energy policies of Premier Lougheed. The hon. member for Halifax (Mr. Stanfield) is in the chamber. When he was leader of his party in

1973 and 1974, I remember his suggesting that the price of oil in Canada should more or less follow the international price. When it comes to oil, the Tories think we should have the world price. However, when it comes to fish, lumber and peat moss, they say we should not follow the world price. What hypocrisy! That is a double standard. They say that Ontario should get the world price for the cars, tractors, chain saws and outboard motors which they manufacture, but the fishermen should not get the world price. I say the fisherman and the lumberman has every right to the world price.
Coming from New Brunswick, I would not for one minute accept a government that would say otherwise. I have defended the government policy we are now following. I would not accept any policy that would restrict the profits of the fishing or lumber industry to the point that their prices or penetration of the market would be diminished. If this went on for a long time, those industries could possibly be asked to make a sacrifice or follow a policy of reinvesting in their mills, plants or whatever they have.
Look at the losses from the bankruptcies that have occurred over the past seven or eight years in the fishing industry in Newfoundland, New Brunswick and the rest of the Atlantic provinces as well as those in the forestry industry. How can anyone suggest that these people should not benefit for a certain period from the currency exchange market?
The policy being followed by the government is a fair policy. I have never heard the leader of the New Democratic Party say that wages in the auto plants in Oshawa should not be at the North American level. Neither have I heard him say that the wages of those who manufacture outboard motors in Peterborough should be lower than the North American wage. The same is true with regard to the manufacture of all kinds of equipment and with regard to the resource industries. Mr. Speaker, for at least 15 years the Atlantic provinces have not had the advantages industry can benefit from, for example a better penetration of American markets, be it in the area of fish, building lumber, pulp and paper, peat moss and minerals, fine paper or generally all areas of resource. One of the reasons for this situation is that the international exchange market presently benefits from Canadian exports.
Mr. Speaker, I think it is fair policy to let those industries expand and create more jobs. Pulp and paper as well as building lumber companies are said to be anticipating one of the biggest years in terms of the number of jobs created, in terms of salaries, in terms of everything. It is going to be one of the biggest years we have had.
Mr. Speaker, I do not see why the Progressive Conservative party and the hon. member for St. John's East would want to oppose that. I do not understand. I told the government on several occasions that I could not support the restrictive measures which could result in those products being sold in Canada at lower prices than on the North American market, and for a very simple reason.
I have never heard the leader of the New Democratic Party and member for Oshawa-Whitby (Mr. Broadbent), who comes from a riding where cars are manufactured, say in this House that car workers in Oshawa should earn less than the average North American salary. If the market today allows fishermen, woodworkers and peat workers to have better wages, Mr. Speaker, I cannot understand why they should not be given a chance. Why come up and say: You, no.
