I would like to say a few words about the comments of the hon. member for Oshawa-Whitby who recommends yet another control policy. However, Mr. Speaker, from his very first days in the House the hon. member for Oshawa-Whitby, like the former leader of his party during the 1972 election, has always submitted all types of distortions and made-up figures to show that when certain companies make big profits, this necessarily means that they are ripping off Canadian consumers.
Mr. Speaker, this is a naive concept of the operation of our economy and does not correspond to reality. If there are no profits in a company, how can this industry or this company keep up with modern technology? Where will it take the necessary funds to expand, to implement modern methods, to protect the jobs and all the other economic benefits that the community in which it is established can enjoy because of it? Where will it get this? The Leader of the New Democratic Party never talks about this. Socialists never answer this question. They simply say that all investments should come from the public sector or that the public sector should borrow for everything. In other words, we should use the taxpayers' money because the public treasury must provide all the funds. We collect taxes or else we borrow on behalf of the taxpayers. What these people are suggesting is that all investments in a society should come from the public sector. How can they expect the private sector to finance the development and modernization of their own plants if they do not make a profit?
An hon. member is shaking his head to show that this is not so, that the public sector can finance everything. I would like to ask him how we can expect banks, financial institutions or those who buy shares on the market to invest in these plants or production units if they are not profitable?
Mr. Speaker, if an industry, sector or plant is to modernize, protect jobs and safeguard the community, as indeed our Canadian communities derive direct and indirect benefits from industrial activity, how can they remain in business without showing a profit? Every time profits increase we are faced with that naive NDP reaction. But members from that party of course never quote direct figures. They never refer to such or such a corporation increasing its profits from say $100,000 to $200,000, which may not be excessive in certain cases. The reference is to say profits soaring 100 per cent.
A 100 per cent increase may be obtained by putting $10 on top of $10, but the increase is still only $10. Mr. Speaker, playing with percentages is really dishonest. It does not give

parliament or the public the true picture. It is misleading the public. When I hear people like the NDP leader and his colleagues comparing 1978 profits, those in the last quarter of 1978 and projections for 1979, with those in 1976 and 1977, this is really dishonest. Truly it is trying to mislead the House and public, because we all know profits were low over that period. Was it not normal then that the increase be significant percentage wise? What counts is the increase in absolute terms. And looking at the profit increase in absolute terms, there may be cases of profiteering, but the broad point cannot be made that all profit increases in Canada over 1978 have been excessive in any given sector. As I say, there may be individual cases, but the broad point cannot be made that all profits have been excessive.
True, Mr. Speaker, food prices have been going up rapidly. True, there has been abnormal increase in that sector right now. Take the case of fish for instance. Fishermen today sell their catch to processors who in turn sell most of their finished product in the United States and Europe. When they sell in the U.S. and Europe they are paid in U.S. or European currency and can command higher prices. What are hon. member asking for? According to the NDP leader, it is unjust that fishermen should have this advantage for a certain time. When a Canadian citizen buys fish, if he can afford it, does he say that fishermen must subsize his food bill? What does he say? Mr. Speaker, I am very happy to be here listening to this debate because I have finally learned why we have an 83-cent dollar. It is because the hon. member for Gloucester (Mr. Breau) is in favour of an 83-cent dollar. He told the government that we must have an 83-cent dollar, and he would oppose any effort to stop the dollar from going down to 83 cents.
I have heard no one from any party in this House take exception to producers getting world prices for their produce except for oil, in which case prices have been held considerably below world prices. The hon. member for Gloucester must feel he has a weak case; otherwise he would not put up such a straw argument. No one is opposed to producers getting world prices for their fish or lumber, but some of us are concerned about what the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) seems to be
Unfair Price Increases
concerned about, if I understand him, and that is that the falling dollar has substantial inflationary effects and causes about one-third of the inflation we have been experiencing in recent months. I think that is something to be concerned about.
The hon. member said the Conservative party is confused. I daresay from time to time we get confused, but we try not to be dishonest. I have to categorize the anti-inflation policy of the government for the last number of years as lacking in frankness, being inconsistent and being opportunistic and basically dishonest. No doubt the hon. member for Gloucester will go to his part of the country taking credit for the advantages of the discount of 17 cents on our dollar. The Prime Minister and others will try to persuade people in other parts of the country that while the government is maintaining somewhat of a dirty float, it is concerned about the declining dollar. They will be saying that this came about in spite of their best efforts to pursue policies which would ensure the strength of the Canadian dollar, because they are concerned about inflationary effects. The Liberal party and the hon. member for Gloucester cannot have it both ways, and they might as well stop trying now because they are going to be exposed.
I understand the reaction of the leader of the New Democratic Party. Going into a supermarket these days is a rather chilling experience, about the same thing as listening to the Minister of Finance (Mr. Chretien) present a budget in this House or hearing about the size of the deficit he is predicting. The leader of the New Democratic Party suggested in this House this afternoon that the way to deal with this situation at the present time is to establish an investigatory commission with power to roll back. I am disappointed in my hon. friend, the leader of the New Democratic Party, because this is really nothing more than a gimmick unless it really amounts to controls.
I suppose in fairness one has to conclude that it does amount to controls. It is easy enough to talk about fair prices and rolling back unfair prices, but what is a fair price and what is an unfair price? We would have to establish some criteria. If a commission is to be established to roll prices back, it has to be given some criteria by this parliament under which to operate. Such a commission would be a form of control. The leader of the New Democratic Party says it really would not be a general control but a selective control.
How in justice can we operate selective controls? When we talk about selective controls, do we mean that some people would have their prices rolled back if they were caught by the commission but other people could gain bigger margins if they could get away with it? Is no one to be subjected to any specific kind of regulation? There must be some concept of fairness, and in all frankness I do not feel it helps the case of the New Democratic Party to talk about selective controls. That would be no more advantageous than general controls.
I do not think there is any way the New Democratic Party can get away from the controls aspect. If this commission is to be something more than a gimmick, it has to control prices effectively. It has to keep price increases within some concept

February 27, 1979
Unfair Price Increases
of fairness to be defined by the Parliament of Canada, and that is surely a form of control.
It seems to me that what we are experiencing here this afternoon is to some extent a replay of 1973 and 1974. In that era, as I recall it, the New Democratic Party was calling for some form of control on prices. The government introduced the profiteering legislation to which the minister referred earlier this afternoon.
I do not want to go through all the history of those days but, as the minister said, that policy was not considered to be appropriate when the government came back with a clear majority and it was not beholden in any way to my friends in the New Democratic Party. The profiteering legislation was clearly a concept adopted by the government of the day in 1973 and 1974 to maintain the support of the New Democratic Party members of this parliament for a limited period of time. When the government came back after the election of 1974 and did not need that support, it dropped the whole idea.
I am not prepared, and I do not believe the members of my party are prepared, to support a return to controls at this time. We have just been through all that with regard to the AIB. It is true that I and my party advocated short term, general controls on prices and incomes back in 1973-74 because we considered them appropriate at that time. We saw the development of a strong degree of inflationary psychology and we advocated controls at that time for the only purpose for which controls are really useful, and that is to curb and deflate inflationary expectations. However, the government, in its wisdom and for electoral purposes, said that controls never work, that they were unalterably opposed to controls, and they fought the campaign on that issue. As we know, after the election we heard no more about the profiteering legislation and the government resorted to controls.
When the control measures were brought in, the government predicted that by the fall of 1978, that is last fall, inflation would be down to some 4 per cent. We know that that has not happened. I do not want to spend too long on the government's record.
I notice all hon. members on the other side are busily engaged in writing and do not want to hear what I am saying. I do not blame them; I would not want, if I were on their side, to listen to a recital of their cynical behaviour either. But regardless of how busy hon. members may keep themselves, the fact is that they have behaved in this way and this is one of the difficulties which the government confronts at the present time.
One of the main difficulties that the country has been facing in terms of inflation, following the removal of the AIB controls, has been the devaluation of the Canadian dollar. This has been recognized by the Prime Minister and by members of the government. The Canadian dollar has been falling because people in the rest of the world do not have confidence in the government or in the Canadian dollar. As the governor of the Bank of Canada said in the Standing Committee on Finance,

Trade and Economic Affairs, he was very concerned that we were getting near the point where any significant further fall in the value of the dollar would trigger the kind of wage demands and general cycle that Great Britain and some other countries have experienced. He emphasized in the committee the grave importance of the Canadian dollar's not taking any further significant drop.
When we consider how we are going to fight inflation, one of our aims surely must be to prevent that drop from happening. The leader of the NDP made his proposal here today. He said the fact that prices are going up may well trigger substantial wage demands. That may well be, but what is the most significant reason that prices have been going up? There may be some profiteering in the country, I do not know, but I do know and I can see there has been a significant fall of the Canadian dollar with consequential effects on price increases. I can see this kind of thing making the working man in this country very nervous about his standard of living and causing him to think twice about the wage settlement he is prepared to accept.
This is not the whole story but I think that to a very substantial extent one thing we have to establish, if we are going to get anywhere, is that we will deal with these problems in a straightforward way. We are not going to go around one part of the country saying that the devaluation of the dollar is a great thing for our exports, and in another part of the country telling some kind of story about doing the best we can to prevent the dollar from falling and indeed to strengthen the dollar. We are not going to introduce a policy, such as the 1975 policy, that "we are going to wrestle the inflation rate down to 4 per cent", and then fail. I do not know if members on the other side have noticed that we have failed, but we on this side of the House see the failure. The realization of that failure is not confined to this House; it is seen all over the world. Anybody trading on the Canadian dollar can see the difference between the promises of this government and the actual performance.
When we first introduced the controls, the government was against any severe fiscal restraint. That was in the fall of 1975. In the summer of 1978, I think, the Prime Minister, perhaps off the top of his head, announced severe fiscal restraint. What kind of consistency is that? Why did he change his mind? Possibly because he figured it was popular in the summer of 1978 to be in favour of fiscal restraint.
When "The Way Ahead" was published and released in the fall of 1976, the government announced its determination to head off any further inflation. I think it claimed the rate of inflation was down to 6 per cent and predicted it would soon be down to 4 per cent. We all know it is up around 9 per cent.
One of the substantial problems that the country faces in maintaining respect for the value of our dollar, in maintaining any respect outside our country for the future of our economy, is the lack of credibility of the government. Yet the government announced a year and a half or so later that it is following a policy diametrically opposed. You have a government making firm predictions as to what effects its policies
February 27, 1979

will have on the rate of price increases in the country, and the actual rate of inflation is more than twice as high as was predicted.
I do not believe there are any easy answers to the economic problems this country faces, economic difficulties which have been brought about in substantial measure by this government. But when you have people playing games, as did the hon. member for Gloucester today, and when you have a Minister of Finance presiding over a budget deficit of some $12 billion, up $1 billion or so from the previous year, and trying to blame that on the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Clark) and saying the Leader of the Opposition was talking about big deficits, what kind of games are these? The members opposite and their ministers have a serious responsibility to tell the people the truth, even in election time.
We have had on the part of the government a sequence of deception and change, and even when the government is trying to be honest, which is not too often, and making predictions about the effect of its policies, it has proved to be incredibly wide of the mark, so wide of the mark as to destroy any confidence on the part of anybody watching this country that the government has the slightest idea as to what it should be doing or what is going on.
A restraint program was introduced when there was a rate of inflation of something over 10 per cent. Three and a half years later we are operating at an inflation rate of over 9 per cent. We have a dollar which has been drifting downwards and the government pretending that the market might determine the level of the dollar when in fact the dollar is floating on a sea of foreign borrowings. Even with all those borrowings, the dollar has drifted down to close to 83 cents. Despite the grave concern the governor of the Bank of Canada expressed about this process, the hon. member for Gloucester stood up in the House and said that this is a terrific thing and tried to invent a straw man to attack.

speakeroldname: Hon. Warren Allmand (Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs):

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have been listening to this debate this afternoon, contrary to what was suggested by the hon. member for Halifax (Mr. Stanfield).

We have subsidized eastern consumers of oil. My colleague has recently increased the guaranteed income supplement and developed a child tax credit of $200 per child to help lower and middle income groups. We have lowered sales and personal income taxes both directly and via indexing. As a matter of fact, the recent consumer price index indicated that the federal sales tax reduction announced in the November budget is being passed on, and that the non-food element

of the recent CPI showed a very slight increase due to that tax cut. As a matter of fact, in some cases there were decreases in the index respecting clothing and furniture.
Foremost in our initiatives to control inflation in recent years was the establishment of the Anti-Inflation Board in the fall of 1975. I want to point out to the House and remind Canadians that that occurred 15 months after the 1974 election, at a time when there was escalating inflation. speechtext: Oh, oh!

speakerposition: Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs
subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-NON-CONFIDENCE MOTION- REQUESTED ESTABLISHMENT OF FAIR PRICES COMMISSION
speechtext:
I was a member of the government and of the House much before the 1974 election when we said that we had a contingency plan for price controls but that we did not think controls should be applied at that time. We did not apply them after the election, but they were applied 15 months later. It was not because we wanted to do it; it was a situation similar to a person requiring a serious operation to cure a very drastic medical problem. We felt we had to go ahead with the controls in the fall of 1975.
In comparing the provisions of that proposal in 1975 with the provision before the House today, it is interesting to note that the Anti-Inflation Board was given the power to investigate and to roll back prices. But what did the NDP do at that time? They voted against the measure unanimously. More than that, half way through the program they attempted to terminate the AIB mandate by circulating a petition. Of course, at that time NDP members said that the AIB program was a program to control wages and not prices and, of course, that was not true. There were guidelines respecting wages, prices and profits. As a matter of fact, there were rollbacks in all areas. Even recently the AIB ordered rollbacks respecting prices and profits in the food industry, in a prominent food chain. Also that was done respecting insurance and other industries. The controls applied to profits and prices as well as wages, but the NDP did not support this policy.
Today the NDP is proposing a system where there would be a rollback similar to the roll-back power in the AIB program, and they want us to support it. I agree with the hon. member for Halifax that it is a gimmick.
When we introduced the AIB program, we did so reluctantly and only on a limited basis for a three-year period. At that time we said that its principal purpose was to break the rampant inflation psychology and to implement some structural changes in our economic system. Among those changes that were pursued were reforms of our competition policy, of which I will say more later, the development of an industrial strategy, some of which has been announced in recent weeks by my colleague, the President of the Board of Economic Development Ministers (Mr. Andras); changes in the international trading system, which are now being pursued in the multinational trade negotiations; and extensive measures taken by the government to curtail its growth and to cut out fat and waste; in other words, to streamline our governmental system.

There is no doubt that there has been an alarming increase in food prices, but it certainly has not been to the extent alleged by the NDP leader and, to my knowledge, not for the reasons stated by him. Yesterday he said that a recent AIB report stated that food prices had increased by 21 per cent over the past year. All I can say is the CPI index put out by Statistics Canada reported a year over year increase of 13.5 per cent for food, and this compared with the general index of the year over year increase for all items of 8.4 per cent. On a monthly basis, last month food increased by 1.9 per cent compared with a general increase in the index of 0.8 per cent.
However, these increases are still too large. They are not as large as stated by the leader of the NDP but they are still too large. We expected large increases at the beginning of this year, particularly due to the cost of imported vegetables and fruits and the removal of the wheat subsidy. With regard to the removal of that wheat subsidy, when we removed it we said we only had limited amounts of money and we felt we had to put it where it was needed most. We took the money we had in such universal subsidy programs as the skim milk program and the wheat subsidy program and put it into programs put forward by my colleague, the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Miss Begin), to channel more money to the middle and lower income senior citizen and the middle and lower income families.
The leader of the NDP also referred to increased profits. Once again he distorted the picture. It is true that there have been increased profits certain segments of the food industry, but on the whole these increased profits are welcomed. In 1976 there were very low if any profits in food processing and distribution have been in accord with historical norms. To see a recovery of this nature is certainly a good thing.
Furthermore, to compare increases in profits, as the leader of the NDP has done, without referring to a base I think is dishonest. As he knows, in the food industry there is very erratic behaviour in respect of profits. Profits are continually going up and down in the food processing and retailing industries and, consequently, if you take the profits from a very low base and judge them with a high period, of course you will get in that period a high increase. But, I put it to the NDP and other hon. members, have they seen one occasion since the war-and I think this is a good thing-when our general wage level has decreased? It has not. We continue to see an increase in wages. I say that is a good thing-

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-NON-CONFIDENCE MOTION- REQUESTED ESTABLISHMENT OF FAIR PRICES COMMISSION
speechtext: In real income?

speakerposition: Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs
subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-NON-CONFIDENCE MOTION- REQUESTED ESTABLISHMENT OF FAIR PRICES COMMISSION
speechtext:
In real income. But to compare that with the increase in profits for limited periods of time without defining your base is dishonest.
Generally an increase in profits heralds a resurgence in the economy. The NDP suggests that these profits are unreasonable and in fact that they are the cause of the rapid price rise. That is what I got from the speech of the leader of the NDP. I have been examining the profit reports in recent months and I have not been able to find any evidence to support this
February 27, 1979

contention. Last summer the Minister of Finance (Mr. Chretien) asked the Anti-Inflation Board to conduct a study of profit margins in the food processing and distribution industries. The AIB report in the fall concluded that the profit margins were not out of line with historical norms in these industries.
Just a few weeks ago the Anti-Inflation Board published an update of its fall report and stated once more that, although profits had increased in the third quarter of last year, they were still not out of line with historic norms.
I think I should refer further to some of the wording of the report. It concluded that in the first nine months of 1978 profit margins in the Canadian food processing and retailing industries had varied little from historic norms. This conclusion is similar to the one presented in the earlier report in the fall in respect of the first six months of 1978. The report went on to say that in the food distribution industry the rate of increase in profits had been more than in food processing, but still that it was not out of line with historic norms.
I doubt if there is any industry in Canada which has been investigated as much as the food industry. I have here a list of some of the inquiries and investigations that have been carried on recently. In 1966 to 1968 we had the royal commission on consumer problems and inflation in the prairie provinces, the Batten commission. In 1967 we had the special joint committee on consumer credit and consumer prices, of which I was a member. In 1957 to 1960 we had the royal commission of price spreads of food products, the Stewart commission. In 1948 we had the royal commission on food prices, the Curtis commission. Then we have in Ontario at the present time the Leach commission. We had in British Columbia in 1977 to 1979 the select standing committee on agriculture which studied the B.C. food industry. We have the Anti-Inflation Board and before that we had the food prices review board. There has been study after study of the food industry, and generally these studies have concluded that there is no one level, no one group of companies, which is ripping off the Canadian consumer.
It is true that from time to time we have prosecuted and had convictions recorded against certain food companies under the combines act. That will always be the case. There will always be some bad actors in the field. But generally speaking there has been no evidence and no conclusion in any report that I know of that any one sector of the food industry is ripping off the consumer.
I should also like to put on record that we have been very active in my department in pursuing action under the combines act regarding such things as price fixing, price discrimination, market rigging, predatory pricing, misleading advertising, double-ticketing and so on, which are all marketing offences and illegal under the Combines Investigation Act. We have been extremely successful in gaining convictions against many companies for these things.
I could give a whole list of activities and initiatives taken by my department to attack price fixing, unfair pricing and misbehaviour in the marketplace. What further can we in government do to deal with escalating prices, especially food prices?
Unfair Price Increases
This afternoon my colleague, the President of the Board of Economic Development Ministers, stated that we are examining ways to strengthen our price monitoring capabilities so we can do a better job. That is already in the works; but it will not involve a control mechanism, nor will it have rollback powers. We are also examining measures to increase food supply where appropriate to moderate food prices, and to encourage Canadians to move to other more reasonable food alternatives.
Recently the government appointed a new chairman of the national food products marketing council, a chairman who has had experience not only in agriculture but also in the consumer movement. She will give a more fair hearing to all elements of the food industry. There were new guidelines produced for the food products marketing council which instructed the council to give a more extensive hearing to, and greater flexibility in the consideration of, these elements. In my department we have several programs to help consumers get the best value for their food dollar. We distribute to many daily and weekly newspapers in the country what is called a "food backgrounder" which provides information on the best way to spend money on food. For example, last week many columns carried information about the price of pork which was a good buy in many parts of the country. At other times protein alternatives have been suggested such as eggs, poultry, fish and so on. This information has been helpful to consumers. We are also establishing as an experiment a phone-in service in Vancouver and Victoria where consumers can call a published number and get information on their problems concerning food and food prices.
During the summer we bring together experts on nutrition and food and then send them to areas of the country where help is needed most-the poor areas of the cities, Indian groups, Indian reservations and remote rural areas, to instruct people on good food, nutrition, and the best value for money.
We are encouraging the development of "no name" generic foods and "no frills" stores. I have visited these stores and tasted and examined the food. This has been a very successful program in selling good food at lower prices. If consumers take advantage of these types of marketing they can save money.
Finally, Mr. Speaker, we intend to bring in very shortly once again, reforms to our competition legislation. If anything will really assure fair prices for the consumer it is a truly competitive and open marketplace. If the opposition parties, in particular, the NDP, really want to see fair prices in the marketplace, then I challenge them to give quick passage to the competition bill when it is brought forward in a few days. It is significant, Mr. Speaker, that no opposition party has approached the government to co-operate on the passage of the competition legislation which would, among other things, move it from a criminal type legislation to civil legislation. This would allow us to proceed with a great deal more flexibility than the present law, and to outlaw and convict on many practices which lead to higher prices and inferior products in the marketplace.

February 27, 1979
Unfair Price Increases
Inflation is a matter of great concern to the government, but the government is also concerned about the flexibility and responsiveness of the Canadian economy. The government is confident that businesses and labour union leaders have the same concern that we not fritter away the gains that we have made through the AIB program over the past three years. Government expenditure is under control; wage demands and negotiated settlements are more realistic; the outlook for our exports is excellent, and there is a strong possibility that food price increases will be more moderate as time goes on.
In these circumstances, to return to confrontation and controls, as the motion before the House proposes, rather than to place greater emphasis on self-restraint and responsibility, would be a move in the wrong direction. Canadians know that they cannot increase their competitiveness and their standard of living simply by raising prices. The government will, of course, not tolerate an irresponsible attitude toward wage and price escalation, nor will it use its control of monetary policy to underwrite such inflationary increases.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-NON-CONFIDENCE MOTION- REQUESTED ESTABLISHMENT OF FAIR PRICES COMMISSION
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-NON-CONFIDENCE MOTION- REQUESTED ESTABLISHMENT OF FAIR PRICES COMMISSION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, today we are dealing with the New Democratic Party motion to set up a fair prices commission to provide some kind of protection to consumers against alarmingly high price increases. I have listened to the spokesmen for the government trying to paint a picture showing that all is well with the world and that all we have to do is practise some self-restraint to prevent an escalating inflationary cycle for the rest of this year.
I think this confirms what many of us in the real world believe, that cabinet is living in a "Never Never Land." Anyone who has shopped for food or paid the home heating bill knows that prices are going up. The picture is not as rosy as the government tries to convey. For the minister to say that the way out of this dilemma is to practise self-restraint, is ludicrous.

speakerposition: Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs
subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-NON-CONFIDENCE MOTION- REQUESTED ESTABLISHMENT OF FAIR PRICES COMMISSION
speechtext: I did not say that.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-NON-CONFIDENCE MOTION- REQUESTED ESTABLISHMENT OF FAIR PRICES COMMISSION
speechtext:
How do we practise self restraint on food prices? Do we give up eating meat, poultry, or fresh vegetables? Are we to do as a Liberal senator advised, and treat vegetables as a luxury, taking them out of the consumer price index? Apparently Canadians should not use fresh vegetables in their daily diet. That is the kind of nonsense we are offered as the solution to our problems. The minister does not mention self-restraint in the pricing policies of business in this country, especially the large corporations.
I want to analyse why we in this party think prices are going up and that the only real way to help customers is to establish an investigative body with power to roll back unrealistic price increases. We all know from published statistics that prices went up by 9 per cent last year over the year before but wages only went up by 6.4 per cent. Workers today have suffered a loss in real income of some 3 per cent in terms of purchasing power. As my leader said, if this trend continues, with prices going up faster than wages, it is inevitable and reasonable that
workers will ask to catch up. There is no reason why they should be the victims of an economy that is increasingly charging them higher prices in their daily lives. There will be a great impetus to catch up. The scenario will be very much like the high inflation we faced in 1973-74.
Let us examine some price increases that affect most Canadians. The most obvious is food prices which have increased by 21 per cent over a year ago, especially in the area of beef and fresh vegetables. We can only find a solution if we examine the causes. The cost of imported food is a tremendously important factor. Because of the lack of a sound national agricultural and food policy we have to rely on more and more food imports, especially fresh vegetables. As our dollar has declined to some 83 cents U.S., we find that we pay more for U.S. vegetables. The lower Canadian dollar pushes the price of food up.
We agree that little can be done immediately about the price of imported food. The long-run solution is to make Canada more self-sufficient in some of the important foods. Good agricultural land is being taken over for industrial development. Farmers are not receiving adequate prices and are being driven out of business. All of this can be attributed to the lack of a food and agricultural policy.
What has the government done in recent months about a food policy? The Conservative party has proposed cutbacks in government spending. The government has been doing flip-flops regarding certain policy changes but it has accepted the idea that restraint and cutbacks are necessary. Consumers feel the consequences of such action. First of all, the government removed the subsidy on wheat used for bread. This should have meant a three to four-cent increase in the price of a loaf, but somewhere along the line the price went up by seven to ten cents. If the subsidy amounted to three or four cents, surely when it was removed consumers had the right to expect the increase in the price would be no more than three or four cents. But something went wrong along the way. We say that as consumers we need some kind of protection against that unfair escalation in price. We have received no answer from the government because there is no economic tool and there is no investigative body to ensure that that kind of price rip-off does not occur.
The same thing happened when the government, again in response to the Conservative concept of government restraint and cutback, took off the subsidy from skim milk powder. As a result the cost of skim milk powder went up some 50 cents a pound. It should be recalled that it is usually low income families who use this milk powder. They are the ones who are faced with the big burden of cost increases.
Government policy on removing subsidies has contributed directly to recent price increases on certain commodities. We, of course, oppose that kind of policy.
There is another reason why prices are going up; farmers are now able to get higher prices for their products. For example, a few years ago we know that the beef raisers were not getting

February 27, 1979

enough money for their product. It was costing more to produce beef than they were getting for it. So they began to slaughter their herds to avoid bankruptcy. That situation caused a shortage. The demand is still with us and the shortage is there in terms of the actual product, and that drives up prices. What is the solution to that? Surely it is to institute a beef marketing program, some kind of a price support program so we will not have this dramatic fluctuation of prices for beef over the years. This has been avoided in the egg industry by having a regulation of production. Surely we could use the same model for the beef industry to even out the ups and downs and to ensure cattlemen will at least get an adequate price and steady income for their product.
As I said, the farmer is getting a higher price for his product and that is another reason for higher prices. Let us take a look at a specific area and try to determine how much is going to the farmer, how much is going to the retailer and to the other people in the food chain line. Let us look at chicken prices. For example, take a frozen full chicken under four pounds. We find that in February, 1979, the price increase over February, 1978, went up from 46 cents a pound to 53 cents a pound. This was a 15 per cent increase to the farmer. However, the retail price over the same period went from 69 cents a pound to $1.18 a pound, or a 71 per cent increase in price. It seems to me that any rational person examining what is causing food price increases would want to zero in on what caused that 71 per cent increase at the retail level. If we examine that we will realize why price increases are rising so dramatically.
Although the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs (Mr. Allmand) protests, every consumer who goes into the supermarket knows that day by day and week by week prices are going up. People want to know if these price increases are justified.
Let us now look at the food dollar. For every dollar spent on food we find that 37 cents goes to the farmer and about 32 cents goes to the retailer. The rest goes to processors, wholesalers and transporters.
The AIB has continued to study some of these retail price increases. It has shown that food store profits increased 37.9 per cent in 1978 over the same period in 1977. Now, the NDP accepts that in the private sector profits have to be made. The point is, are the profit increases justified on sound economic grounds which anyone would accept? Has productivity increased thereby justifying a profit increase of that magnitude? Have sales increased, thereby justifying that kind of profit increase?
Again, when one looks at the retail food sector study done by the AIB, they said that profits increased over 37 per cent but the sales only increased by 17.4 per cent. In other words, their profits more than doubled their sales increase. So unless there was a dramatic increase in the productivity at that level, I think we are justified in raising the question, as consumers: is there an unjustified price increase taking place in order to account for that tremendous profit increase, despite a lower sales increase? Surely that is something a fair prices commission which we are advocating today could look at and deter-
Unfair Price Increases
mine whether the consumer was being ripped off by unjustified price increases. The price increases in the food industry are only one symptom of what is happening to the economy.
In the House I have raised the question of lumber price increases. These prices have gone up 70 per cent over the past two years, 10 per cent in the month of January, 1979 alone. I have tried to get the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs to investigate that problem, and where necessary bring in representatives of the companies and force a moderation in price or even a rollback, but this has been to no avail. Let us not fool ourselves. This price increase for lumber will cause a tremendous increase in the cost of housing. With this increased price for lumber I have estimated that it will cause about a $1,200 increase in the cost of an ordinary single family dwelling consisting of 1,800 square feet of floor space.
The minister says that it is the old case of supply and demand; that there is a tremendous demand for lumber products; that the Americans are buying our lumber and this is pushing the price up. He says we are exporting so much because our dollar is low and that we are making a good buck when the Americans buy our lumber. This was supposed to be a rationale for the lower dollar to help Canadians in terms of exports. But what has it done? It has pushed up the price of lumber in Canada for the Canadian consumer. This government has not taken the logical step of introducing a two-price system for lumber so that Canadian domestic consumers would pay a lower price. The lumber exported could fetch a price at what the market would bear on the world market and so allow that price to increase. I see no justification why Canadian consumers should face a 71 per cent increase in the cost of lumber when we all know the cost of production has not gone up by any kind of percentage relationship to that price increase.
Steel prices are another example. The price of steel is so important to our economy it touches on items all the way from pots to automobiles. The big three steel companies have recently increased their prices anywhere from 5 per cent to 18 per cent. As a result, these steel companies have recorded a 46 per cent profit increase, from $196 million in 1977 to $285 million in 1978. Last August, of course, steelworkers who are employed by these companies, and whose hard work contributed to this profit, had to accept a 6 per cent to 7 per cent wage increase, despite 9 per cent inflation and record company profits.
The Liberals and Conservatives in this House like to blame workers' wages as the main cause of companies raising prices. I disagree fundamentally with that. My argument is that companies today are able to manipulate prices upwards because our supposed free enterprise or competitive system in reality is no longer working. We do not have effective competition to hold down prices in Canada today. What we do have is a state of oligopolies or near monopolies. We have a few large companies controlling their particular sector of the economy. When they are able to control it through supply, they are able

Unfair Price Increases
to control it through price. We have some 200,000 corporations in Canada, but a mere 500 of them accounted for 51 per cent of the sales, 59 per cent of the assets, and 63 per cent of the profits. Can anyone tell me we have effective competition in our economy when that kind of situation occurs?
If we do not have effective competition, we will not have fair prices to the consumer. Where is the competition when only four companies in Canada control 70 per cent of all flour and cereal production, four companies control 75 per cent of our iron and steel production, four companies control 93 per cent of our motor vehicle production, four companies control 71 per cent of all agricultural machinery production, four companies control 53 per cent of all slaughtering and meat products industries, and four companies control 79 per cent of all petroleum refining in this country?
There is no effective competition when you have that kind of control by the few over these important sectors of our economy. As John Galbraith, the economist, said, if the market fails, so does the case against government intervention. That is why the NDP wants a fair prices commission set up by the federal government, with powers on a national scope to investigate price increases on a selective basis where it becomes apparent to the consumer that there are tremendous increases, and this commission should have the power to roll back unjustified price increases.
The market will not do it for us because there is no longer effective competition in the major sectors of the market. If that will not work, the only protection we as consumers have is for the government to step in and act on our behalf through the commission we are advocating in this debate today.
As I said, we recognize that private companies have to make a profit, but where the market is not working it is incumbent upon government to analyse and see whether the profits are excessive or not, and whether they are justified in relation to the costs of production. Until we have a fair prices commission we will not be able to counteract the natural temptation of these large and powerful corporations which control so much of our economy to jack up prices arbitrarily, charging whatever they figure the market will bear.
If prices go up, inflation goes up, and workers demand more in wage increases. The vicious cycle repeats itself. The corporations have done very well since 1972. When you subtract the effect of inflation over the period 1972 to 1978, you find that corporate profits have increased in real terms by 55 per cent while wages have only increased by 10 per cent in real terms.
Throughout the debate here the Liberals and Conservatives have indicated they oppose the NDP motion to set up a fair prices commission to protect consumers. I regret the stand of the two old line parties, although it does not surprise me. The Conservative answer to the problem of rising prices is to call an election and get rid of the government. They do not propose any alternative solution other than the time-worn idea of wage and price controls. The Liberals stole the idea from the Conservatives. We know how ineffective that program was and how it disrupted the economy and penalized workers. The

President of the Board of Economic Development Ministers (Mr. Andras) says that profits are good, that he agrees with what is happening, leaving the consumer to the mercy of a market controlled by these near monopolies. I consider that unfair.

Mr. Speaker, just before the dinner break I was making a few comments concerning the motion put before the House by the Leader of the New Democratic Party (Mr. Broadbent) today. I think it is important that we read the wording of the motion once again. It states:
That, given the government's failure to hold down rising prices, which have increased the cost-of-living burden for Canadian families, this House calls on the government to establish a Fair Prices Commission, with powers to investigate and, where necessary, to roll back unfair price increases.
The reason I read that motion, Mr. Speaker, is that until we can think of the true import of what he is saying we cannot conceive of the total inconsistency of the socialists to my left. Here we have them saying that the government has failed- which we agree-to hold down rising prices, and in turn these prices have increased the cost-of-living burden to Canadians. Certainly nobody on this side of the House would disagree with that. But how the leader of the NDP can fail to realize that his group was instrumental in triggering the government into the spending programs and deficit programs which have resulted in the inflation we are now living under in this country, I find hard to understand.
The motion then goes on to call on the government to establish a fair prices commission with powers to investigate. If such a commission were ever set up, the first thing it should start investigating is why the NDP voted so often to support the government during the minority days of the parliament between 1972 and 1974. If that commission was ever established I hope it would analyse why the NDP, in spite of the fabulous monetary and fiscal growth on the part of the government, continued to support it if, at that time, they were worried about inflation. The fact is, anybody could have predicted then that this alliance between the socialists and the near-socialists was going to trigger the inflation we are now experiencing.
We do not need a commission to tell us there is inflation in our country. Any housewife can go into a corner grocery store and see the price increases. If he cannot afford the 25 cents it now costs to buy a copy of the Globe and Mail I will give my copy to the Leader of the NDP and perhaps he could read the
Unfair Price Increases
livestock reports which appear there. He could see, for example, that in Omaha the price for No. 1 cattle is between $65 and $67 per hunderweight live weight. If he looks at this, he will find that in Montreal the same type of animal sells for $75 to $80. If he does some arithmetic, he will find that it takes 120 cents to buy one American dollar. If he multiplies the Omaha price by 120 Canadian cents, he will get exactly the price beef is trading for in Montreal, Toronto or Calgary compared with Omaha. In short, as far as live beef is concerned, our prices are 20 per cent higher because the dollar is 17 per cent below par with the American dollar. It is as simple as that.
How these fellows can seem to be so mystified and run around saying they do not know where inflation is coming from, and how they can say they want a commission to explain it is not hard to understand. The truth is that they want a decoy. They want to be able to go to the Canadian electorate and pretend that they have in mind the setting up of a fair prices commission which somehow would do something meaningful about inflation. That is just a blind. It is not fair to the Canadian public. They know this might help some of their bureaucratic friends to get new and high paying jobs, but we will not do one thing to solve the problem of inflation until we can convince the government of the day, hopefully a Joe Clark government, that prices can be controlled only by restraint in government spending and monetary growth.
It is the government which has the control, but is it not interesting that when this same NDP group was given a chance in November of 1975 to change the AIB reference so that the board could investigate government spending, the NDP voted against us? Hon. members might recall that at that time I moved a motion that the AIB should have power to make explicit, and I quote:
-such implications of the failure of the federal government to co-operate in combating inflation by monitoring the respective main and supplementary estimates of expenditures for each fiscal year of such government, and publicly commenting, within 21 days after any such estimates, are made public, upon any failure, disclosed in such estimates, by such government to combat inflation.
That is what we in this party proposed in November of 1975. We voted for that, but the grand old alliance between the socialists and the near-socialists ganged up on us so there could be no inquiry into the increasing estimates of government expenditures. It is not difficult to understand what has happened since that time. That was in 1975, and in that year total federal government spending was $34,357 billion. Just last week the President of the Treasury Board (Mr. Buchanan) revealed that estimates of government spending are now up to $52 billion.
On budget night, November 16, the deficit predicted for this year by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Chretien) was $12.1 billion. The minister revealed that for fiscal 1980 the deficit would be $12.9 billion. In two short years, the minister tells us, the total deficit is to be $25 billion on an expenditure of roughly $100 billion. In short, for every dollar the government now spends it receives only 75 cents in revenue. The remaining

25 cents have to be found some place, either through debt or through the printing of more money.
That is what is contributing to inflation in this country because, to the degree the government is over-inflating our money system, it causes pressure on prices. To the degree that the deficit is viewed around the world as irresponsible fiscally, that brings our dollar under pressure. And when I say that the dollar is under pressure, let us not forget that since December, 1976, it is not just that our dollar has fallen 16 per cent in relation to the American currency; it has fallen 37 per cent in relation to United Kingdom currency, 47 per cent in relation to the German Deutsche mark, and 74 per cent in relation to the Japanese yen.
That has been the consequence of the irresponsible fiscal and monetary policies this government has put in place in the last four to five years. That is why we are saying we do not need any more decoys. We do not need more commissions to tell us the obvious. What we need most of all is a new government.

speechtext:
If we cannot get rid of the emperor and his hordes, at least let us talk some sense to them. It is the diving dollar which is causing the inflation which is now so objectionable in the country, and let there be no doubt that we do not need a commision to tell us what the full impact of that falling dollar will be. We can talk to any merchant today. I was talking earlier to a manufacturer and distributor in Vancouver. He told me that only now is he starting to pass on the total cost of the goods he has been purchasing from Taiwan, Japan and other oriental countries, and translating the fall in the value of our dollar into higher prices to the Canadian public. Those prices are still to be felt in Canada.
I spoke to a shoe manufacturer in Quebec city at noon today. He said that the public will not believe the prices it will be required to pay for shoes as a result of our collapsing dollar. He pointed out that leather prices have doubled because, since our dollar started to fall, leather became more attractive to buyers in, for example, Japan. They have been buying our leather, and the result is that the price of leather has doubled. The net result is that when we come to buy shoes-which the chap from Quebec city pointed out were manufactured 15 years ago for less than $15-retailers will be paying $60 and, it is anticipated, consumers will be paying $100 per pair. Those are the facts. A head of lettuce today costs 20 per cent more, simply because this government has irresponsibly allowed our dollar to collapse. Let us tell the public the truth and stop pretending some fair prices commission will discover why prices are going up. Prices are going up because this government has failed to run our economy in a responsible way.
I could go through any number of items which are produced and consumed in Canada, but they are priced on a continental basis, and the result is that to the degree our dollar continues to fall Canadian workers are expected to pay American dollar prices, yet they get Canadian dollar wages. That is the dilem-

ma, and surely even this government can realize that it has toyed with a falling dollar. The Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce (Mr. Horner) once said that a 90-cent dollar was a good thing. The government should have had the courage to structure our monetary and fiscal position to ensure that the dollar did not fall below 90 cents and down to the 83-cent level it is at now.
I think every member in this House should go out and start telling the Canadian public the way it is. It is time the public understood that wage and price controls did not work. If we compare our record with that of the United States, we find that in each of the three years when we had wage and price controls and the Americans did not, they performed better than we did as far as inflation control was concerned. Here are the figures. In 1976 the United States had inflation of 5.8 per cent, and we had 7.5 per cent. In 1977 the United States had 6.5 per cent, and we had 8 per cent. In 1978 the United States had 7.6 per cent inflation and we had 9 per cent. With wage and price controls we lost every year.
Hon. members will recall that October day when the Prime Minister announced his wonderful program to control inflation in this country. He said that he would do four things. He was going to bring in wage and price controls. He was going to have government expenditure restraint, monetary restraint, and a massive deregulation of industry. Unfortunately, once the government put its wage and price control program into effect, it forgot, in any meaningful way, the other three points of its restraint program. Government spending, as I have indicated, continued to rise. Certainly the monetary growth continued, and there has been nothing but verbiage so far as deregulation is concerned. That is why we have inflation.
For the NDP to be suggesting now that they want still another commission to control something further shows how out of touch they are with reality. It is not just that they are out of touch with Canadian reality. I referred earlier to the fact that initially they took their approach from the Labour party in England. That is in effect from where they pirated most of their thinking. But unfortunately the lines of communication seem to have broken down because the English Labour party has at least come to its senses, while the NDP charges on in its usual irresponsible way. I say this because I find it is interesting now that when you look at the economic progress report published by the treasury in Great Britain you find that they are taking a meaning approach to expenditure restraint. They have accepted that the growth should be limited to 2 per cent on a real base year over year, and they have projected ahead to 1983 to show that in fact they will keep a lid on their expenditures, they will have a smaller deficit and, in short, that is why the U.K. pound is going up and our dollar is going down. We are the last of the western nations to accept the basic principle that you have to run a prudent economy if you want to lick inflation.

speechtext:
Tonight, Mr. Speaker, the motion before the House deals with the creation of a fair prices commission with powers to investigate and, where necessary, to roll back unfair price increases. To me, Mr. Speaker, this motion is not complete. We are wondering whether it proposes to freeze wages and prices like in the past or whether it is simply designed to study rocketing wages and prices. And we, too, are wondering how to achieve that goal. The mover of that motion did not specify how he intended to reach the objectives contemplated in his motion.
Tonight I would like to make three or four brief proposals which have already been made here and which our party puts forward to stop ever higher prices and wages and so on. This would be done first through the consumer discount, second by the establishment of a commission which would be called the national credit bureau, and third, the reduction of interest or the stoppage of debt accumulation and the control of monopolies.
Most Canadians, Mr. Speaker, have heard of the consumer discount, mainly from us who advocate the reforms of social credit. However, few understand the mechanism. What is the consumer discount? It is simply something that would make prices a reflection of the true economic conditions of the country. In other words, if production is abundant and easy, the purchase of that same production would become easy. So you see that it is not necessary to restrict or even reduce production as is being done today to stabilize prices.
What is wrong with the present make-up of prices? Prices are too high compared to the incomes to pay for them. The imbalance between what is sold and what people can buy leads to economic bottlenecks, waste and material insecurity. That frantic race after higher salaries because prices keep going up produces galloping inflation which will stop only when governments will take the means to stop that rise.
Where do prices come from? Consumer prices come from the total cost of production to which profits and interests must be added. Today the manufacturer says that salaries are too high, the materials he needs to make the end products are also too high and consequently his profits are too low. If he has to raise the cost of his product, the worker in turn will not have the necessary salary to purchase that same product. The fair prices commission as proposed tonight at both the consumer and producer level might probably to able to roll back certain unjustified and unjustifiable price increases.
But in addition to that monitoring board, the hon. member for Oshawa-Whitby (Mr. Broadbent) would have been better off including in his motion the consumer discount to reduce injustices. The consumer discount would work this way: prices paid by consumers for their purchases would be discounted by the retailers who, after submitting to a government agency the necessary proof that the sales were actually made, would
Unfair Price Increases
receive credits to compensate the difference between the discounted prices and normal sales prices. Here is an example. Let us say that you want to buy a pair of gloves at the regular price of $20. The retailer who is registered under the consumer discount program will give you a discount of 25 per cent, $5 which the government would pay back to the retailer, or still it would be possible to purchase directly from the retailer if he agreed to reduce his prices.
Ever since we have been sitting in his House, we have been advocating the consumer discount. From the early days of social credit, we had an item in our election platform which reads as follows: a social credit government would reduce consumer goods prices through subsidies paid to retailers provided they lowered their prices by a percentage equivalent to the amount of the subsidies.
This mechanism will eliminate inflation while guaranteeing fair prices. Of course, we would need a commission, which could be called for instance the national credit commission, and which should be quite independent from political influence, as are now Statistics Canada and the Supreme Court of Canada. This commission would be responsible for collecting all the data and figures required for a national account book where it could find all the information necessary to issue credit.
These national accounts would give credit value to all valuable goods in the country whose total could be evaluated in dollars. This evaluation would cover lands, businesses, farm industries, public buildings, houses, mines, all means of transport, including railroads, ships, airplanes, cars, roads, bridges and canals, as well as our semi-finished and finished products. In other words, it would include as far as possible all material wealth. It should be noted in passing that the census of nearly all these values is already done by Statistics Canada. If we go back to the year 1929, which was more normal than all the others that followed, and if we consider that the figures do not include the value of our undeveloped natural resources, the total of our tangible resources was still evaluated at $30,276 million. This independent commission would be strictly responsible for keeping the national accounts up to date. This means that it would have to register regularly all increases and decreases in our total wealth.
Let us suppose that in a six-month period, we produced or imported $4 billion worth of goods and that improvements costing $200 million were made to our commercial or industrial equipment. This would mean an increase in our national wealth and would be added on the credit side of our national accounts. Let us suppose, on the contrary, that during the same six-month period, consumption and exports amounted to $3.5 billion and that the depreciation of the same equipment amounted to $150,000. This would mean a decrease in our national wealth. This amount would therefore have to be

subtracted from the national accounts or debited to the country.
Mr. Speaker, how could we achieve a balance between the amount of the wealth produced and the amount of money needed for distribution? The Social Credit Party of Canada would suggest the creation of a commission or central bureau responsible for achieving this balance. A federal office of the Social Credit Party of Canada compiles the total wealth produced during the last period on the basis, let us say, of the previous year. It also evaluates total consumption during the same period. The difference provides the available assets which are registered under the available national credit. Mr. Speaker, I have here a chart which gives concrete examples of all this, but I will simply mention a few figures since I cannot table the whole chart.
Let us suppose a production of $7 billion with imports of $1.2 billion and an appreciation of $4.6 billion for a total of $12.8 billion. On the other hand, the consumer account shows $5.5 billion for consumption, $1.2 billion for exports and a depreciation of $1.3 billion, for a total of $8 billion. There is therefore $4.8 billion in the national account for redistribution to consumers. I quote:
A few additional remarks to clarify this. Imports and exports were set at equal levels, although this will not always be the case, but this must be the ultimate goal in a sound system. The purpose of international trade is to give consumers access to a greater variety of goods, not to draw the last cent out of customers. The money-grubbing merchant whose aim, in international trade, is to pocket his neighbour's gold is the unnatural fruit of a twisted tree.
This gives you an idea, Mr. Speaker, of the second reform we propose, the national credit office, which would have control over investments and especially over consumer prices as well as control over production costs.
Our third suggestion-and I see that my time is fast running out-would be to reduce interest. I think, Mr. Speaker, that we have many times stood before this House to request that interest be either reduced or frozen, especially in the residential construction sector.
Imagine a young man who dreams of building a house nowadays. He must first pay taxes and then, because the value of the dollar drops, he loses another 17 per cent. He must pay a building tax, excise tax, and sales tax, so that before thinking of building a house he must think of the 48 per cent in taxes alone that he must pay. He buys building materials and builds himself a $40,000 house which in reality is worth only $20,000. The cost includes $20,000 worth of taxes. He then goes to a a loan company and obtains from the Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation or any other agency a 30-year loan at 10 per cent, 11 per cent, or 11.5 per cent. At the end of 30 years, he will have paid four times the nominal value of his $40,000 house which in fact contains only $20,000 worth of materials. He will have paid $40,000 to build his house and $160,000 to financial institutions because he will have succeeded in building it.
This is why I suggest that a young man who wants to build a house today must be realistic and say: I am going into debt today not for $40,000 but $160,000. Mr. Speaker, if on top of that we add municipal taxes, school taxes and insurance coverage, we realize that it is costly nowadays for someone who wants to build a home.
Well, I think that if the government decided once and for all to use the credit of the Bank of Canada to finance those houses and desisted from making those young couples pay two, three or four houses to own one after 30 years, we would not need urban development and housing programs to encourage young people to build, although I say to encourage young people to get into debt, because we know ahead of time that 50 per cent of those young people will never overcome their debts. That is why I ask and propose today, while we are debating this motion, that the government pass a legislation to allow those who want to build a single family dwelling to do so, and to pay one but not three or four houses in interest. Only then, Mr. Speaker, could we urge people to build their houses.
Finally, I would like to say a few words on debts, as long as the government continues to get into debt and set such an example. In the fourth quarter of last year we borrowed $7 billion, again we are borrowing $10 billion, and that is over and above our $12 billion deficit, and the bigger the better.
It is raining billions around here, but billions of dollars of debts, and until such time as we have put an end to that type of indebtedness, and as long as the Minister of Finance (Mr. Chretien) keeps on saying, as he did recently in reply to a question: "We are not that deep into debt; we have committed only 33 per cent of the gross national product," the situation will not change. Moreover, the minister is not telling the truth to the people. He compares the debt of the federal government with the gross national product. Let him compare eggs with eggs, and apples with apples. When he speaks of the gross national product, let him compare it with the national debt.
Mr. Speaker, if we take all the debts of the federal government, the provinces, school boards, municipalities and individuals, we will find that our national debt exceeds by perhaps $25 billion our gross national product. To be sincere, frank, and in order not to mislead the population, when we speak of the gross national product, we must compare it with the national debt and not with the debt of a single municipality or a single province. I see that I have run out of time.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I welcome the opportunity to take part in this debate on a subject which is extremely important to all Canadians, and particularly to Canadians of low income. I welcome particularly the very practical measures announced in the course of today's debate by the President of the Board of Economic Development Ministers (Mr. Andras) and by the Minister of
(Mr. Gauthier (Roberval).]
February 27, 1979

Consumer and Corporate Affairs (Mr. Allmand), which of the many remedies available place emphasis on a strengthened monitoring group, on increased competition in the market, and also on increasing the food supply and the information about alternatives. Information to consumers about alternatives is perhaps a counter-inflationary measure which is not generally as well perceived as it might be, but quite clearly the better informed the consumer, the better he or she can protect himself or herself.
The concern being expressed by Canadians about high food prices at the present time is very understandable. Food is a necessity of life. Escalation of food costs faces people day in and day out when they shop for their families. Consumers on the average spend 13.2 per cent of their disposable incomes on food for the home, but about 17 per cent of the population which makes up the lowest income sector spends nearly one quarter of its income on food. This is the group for whom recent price increases create a grave problem, the people who have little discretionary income and little flexibility.
In the search for solutions I think it is important to think of future supply as well as costs in the here and now. Intelligent consumer advocacy requires a concern for supply as well as for costs. For example, at the present time butter, skim milk powder and cheese are showing some price increases, but since these reflect increased prices to the farmers who produce industrial milk as of January, 1978, these prices should promote confidence among producers and provide stability in the industry so that all Canadians can benefit from a steady supply of dairy products.
The high cost of beef at the present time is related to supply problems. Beef prices have risen again and are expected to do so in the future because supplies of beef in North America are declining as cattlemen retain animals to rebuild their herds.
Farm prices have risen rapidly since December and this is being reflected in retail prices. Low prices are not necessarily in the consumer's best interests if they are reached at the expense of prejudicing supply in the future. In the past the Government of Canada has intervened to keep prices down in the short term by subsidies on flour and skim milk powder for instance. The difficulty with the subsidy route is that it is universal and benefits equally those with very high incomes and those whose incomes are very limited. With present government emphasis on restraint and relocation, the decision has been made to help those who need help most by, instead, trying to put more disposable income into the hands of people with lesser incomes so they are better able to withstand increases in food costs and other things related to the necessities of life.
As part of this emphasis we have seen the indexing of personal exemptions under the Income Tax Act, the child tax credit, increased family allowances, and increases in the guaranteed annual supplement. Putting money into the hands of those who most need it in order that they can meet the necessities of life is my preferred method of dealing with this kind of inflation in respect of basic necessities.
Unfair Price Increases
It is a matter of regret to me that a couple of years ago when the then minister of national health and welfare wanted to introduce a system of subsidy for the working poor, the province of Ontario blocked that measure, just as Ontario blocked the proposal made to allow housewives to protect their Canada Pension Plan contributions during the years when they were at home with children, receiving low or no income which would allow them to protect their buying power in future years when they are retired.
However, basic to any increase in social service payments is, of course, a strong, healthy economy. That is why I welcome the structural changes in the economy that have been made in the last year or two and with which we are now progressing, the industrial strategy measures, the current negotiations with GATT, the reduction in government expenditures in order to leave more room in the private sector and, particularly, our decision to go ahead with some amendments to the competition bill.
The food industry is one that has been investigated more than any other, and this afternoon the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs listed some of the many investigations we have had, none of which has produced serious or pervasive evidence of price gouging. There have been some rollbacks under the AIB program of food prices, and there have, indeed, been some convictions for double ticketing or misleading advertising, but essentially as one looks at the long history of investigations into the food industry, and the comparatively small amount of evidence of dishonest practices that ran afoul of present legislation, one has to ask oneself why the public continues to be so suspicious of retailers and distributors in the food industry. I think I can see two or three reasons for this.
When a worker, a union, or a consumer looks at profit in the manufacturing sector, there is perhaps less tendency to regard it as necessarily negative. There is more of an assumption that profits in the manufacturing sector may go into plant expansion or something that will create more jobs. When profit is made by a large supermarket it is not so easy to assume it will be used to benefit Canadians generally, and to create jobs. Most people would think that the logical place for supermarket profits to be reflected would be in reduced prices.
There is also the fact that people are faced with food costs every day. There is not the same opportunity for discretion as there may be with some manufactured items. In the food industry, practices which are not dishonest in themselves can distort the market. There are practices against which we have no legislation at the present time, and the commission which the Ontario government now has investigating the question of volume discounts is perhaps a response to this kind of concern.
Profit recovery has traditionally heralded a general economic recovery, but profits in the food industry are generally regarded not as an indicator of good things to come but as an indicator of lack of adequate competition.

I say that that in effect shows the Tories are also verbally obfuscating the public. They are not prepared to challenge the corporate sector. The corporate sector must be challenged. And what do I mean by that? I mean in effect that the government instead of standing back on the sidelines and reacting in a neutral sort of way, must involve itself in planning this economy and directing it. It has left it to the multinational corporate sector.
As I observe the scene today, mergers are taking place and the corporate giants are getting larger and larger. They are getting more powerful than those who are elected to govern the country. The corporate sector must be challenged in this country. For example, when Inco made a $300 million net profit in 1973 there was nothing incumbent upon them to invest that profit in Canada. What did they do? They bought a battery company in the United States. They did what they felt was in the best interests of the corporate structure, and they were taken to the cleaners by their stockbrokers. Corporations are not in business to create employment. They are not some sort of social agency to look after the welfare of Canadians. They are there to maximize profits.
It is in the interest of the government to make sure that the resources of this country are so dispersed, so invested as to create a healthy economic climate for our people. We are not the servants of the multinational corporate structures. It is the reverse, and roles have been changed in this place. For example, a cabinet minister takes the same plane with bankers to Toronto. So how do you expect him to take a tough stand with them, Mr. Speaker? What happened to the legislation that would amend the combines act, and the Small Loans Act?
