The argument is that the rate must be made high enough for banks to lend money. These are the people who made a billion dollars in profit last year. I am talking about the big five. They have all sorts of money to invest in sound investments in Chile and Guatemala. They really have good credit ratings. And yet the banks do not have money to lend to Canadians at 34 per cent or 24 per cent interest; instead, they wanted 70 per cent. I say to the minister, bring in a bill that is void of all those sorts of give-aways to the corporate sector and we will give it passage.
Where is the bill which demanded that the banks pay interest on a minimum daily balance? As hon. members know, the banks at present only pay interest on the minimum monthly balance, and that is paid on a quarterly basis. Where is the bill? Where is the bill that said that banks must pay on a minimum daily balance?
Where is the bill directing the banks to take part of their portfolios to set aside for the building of homes for low income and middle income Canadians? Where is that? The government does not dare touch the banks. There is a conspiracy of silence in this House of Commons, and the Tories, who are supposed to be the official opposition in this House, are silent on these matters which affect the welfare and the well-being of the Canadian people.
We have been hewers of wood and drawers of water. As long as people in Canada keep electing Liberal governments, or Tories as alternatives, we will continue to be enslaved in that fashion. Look at what is happening with the falling dollar. Sure our raw resources are now very attractive. To balance our accounts this country is going to sell off more and more resources, forever locking us into that pattern of hinterland development. That is shocking and shameful on the part of this government. If it had any guts at all it would plan the economy so that the investment would be directed into those sectors which are job-creating and which hold some future for Canadians.
We are not going to go on ripping nickel out of the ground. We do not have any research and development for copper and nickel in the Sudbury basin, but the price of nickel is going up and so is the price of copper. The price of cobalt is going up too. Who is getting the benefit from these rising prices?

February 27, 1979

Certainly not the Canadian people, because mining of minerals is capital intensive not job intensive. The job intensive area is in the manufacturing sector.
What kind of planning does the Canadian government have? There is no planning. So as the foreign demand for our resources rose because of the drop in the value of the Canadian dollar, we have to ship more minerals out of the country. The multinational corporations jacked the price up and Canadians pay more as well. We do not have a two-price system.
We do not have a two-price system for lumber. The demand is high because the Japanese want more of our first-class lumber, but Canadians are the ones who pay. Canadians have witnessed a fantastic increase in the price of lumber. That adds to the cost of building a home. However, the friendly banker is right there waiting to give you a mortgage that will be amortized over 40 years. If you wish to retire the mortgage, however, there is a prepayment charge. Where is the bill to eliminate prepayment charges on mortgages?
There is a silent conspiracy. If credit unions can give a no prepayment mortgage, why can the big five not do the same when you retire your mortgage? Why have they hidden that bill? I challenge the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs to bring forward that bill tomorrow, without cooking it up with his banking friends, and we will give it quick passage.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-NON-CONFIDENCE MOTION- REQUESTED ESTABLISHMENT OF FAIR PRICES COMMISSION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I believe the motion before the House tonight is deceptive. I think it is cruel and hypocritical. Therefore I will vote against it. It is deceptive because it is designed to appeal to everyone when it speaks of and rightly condemns unfair prices. Obviously in a time of great hardship, high taxes, high inflation, high prices and high unemployment, any unfair price is one of many elements that may be present in our economy which a thinking people and all MPs are against. I do not care what side of the House the member sits on, everyone in this House is obviously against unfair prices.
As a political slogan or a conscientious and compassionate citizen, all of us in this House and every thinking citizen are against unfair prices. All of us are against the very idea of those who may be able to manipulate the marketplace to their advantage and to the detriment of everyone else. Make no mistake about it. These are very general and genuine concerns today. There may well be abuses in the marketplace.
When one goes food shopping, for instance, and sees week after week large increases in some of the food items in the stores and supermarkets, some of them seasonal items but many of them of the non-seasonal variety, any shopper in Canada today has to wonder whether some of the increases can be justified or whether somewhere, in the long and complex food industry chain from basic producer right through to you and I, the ultimate consumer, there is not someone who is using some unseen and unknown advantage to make an undue profit and produce an unfair price.
Just last weekend in the golden horseshoe area of southern Ontario, which has the reputation of having the most competitive supermarket and grocery industry in the country, resulting in the lowest prices for most food items in the country, I had to worry, along with the mover of the motion, when I noticed that a single fresh imported cauliflower cost me, while doing the family shopping, $1.89. That price was mentioned earlier.
February 27, 1979

What was not mentioned was that when I went to buy four unripe tomatoes, it cost me over SI, more than 25 cents each. We are great salad fans. When I went to buy a single lettuce imported from Holland, of all places, it cost me 89 cents. For three Florida grapefruit the price was 99 cents, and at that I think it was a special, 33 cents for each grapefruit. There are other items with which I shall not bother the House tonight. But I hope no one will go away believing that right now the people of Canada are not concerned about high prices, prices which many of them immediately translate, rightly or wrongly, into the proposition that they are unfair prices.
I repeat, however, that I feel the motion before the House is deceptive. It is misleading, and therefore it is cruel to many people who will be taken in by the type of argument we have just heard from one of the members of the New Democratic Party. Why? Because it was based upon the undeniable fact that the prices of many commodities are higher than most of us have ever seen in our lives, and it is easy to believe that those higher prices could be unfair prices.
Why is the motion deceptive? It is deceptive because, after describing the symptoms correctly, after diagnosing the illness in the Canadian economy, it holds out as its shining beacon, as its gleaming hope, as its cure, a solution which is not only incorrect and ineffective but which is unnecessary-a phony answer, a phony solution. What is the solution it proposes? It is the setting up of yet another restrictive board or commission.
I don't care whether it is called an anti-inflation board or a prices review board, or a centre for the study of inflation and productivity; I don't care whether it is called a fair prices commission or an unfair prices commission, it is certainly not the way to cure the sickness in Canada's price structure or in the nation's economy. I suspect the mover of the motion knows this as well as you and I know it, Mr. Speaker. How can you roll back prices unless you roll back profits and dividends?

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-NON-CONFIDENCE MOTION- REQUESTED ESTABLISHMENT OF FAIR PRICES COMMISSION

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-NON-CONFIDENCE MOTION- REQUESTED ESTABLISHMENT OF FAIR PRICES COMMISSION

speechtext: Spoken like a Liberal!

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-NON-CONFIDENCE MOTION- REQUESTED ESTABLISHMENT OF FAIR PRICES COMMISSION

To determine what is an unfair price, the prices of all ingredients, all the prices involved, would have to be determined. Whether you like it or not, this process has eventually to become a full-fledged control program, a program of control over wages and costs as well as prices. In my naivete, in my innocence of what goes on here, in my belief that there should be some standards and principles in Canadian politics, I thought that the New Democratic Party,
Unfair Price Increases
mainly at the urging of organized labour, was against programs of that type. But here they are, contrary to the expressed wish of the Canadian Labour Congress, the UAW, the steelworkers, CUPE and many others in the organized labour movement, defending a policy which has not worked in the past and which will not work in the future, either.
The mover of the motion says his commission could be operated by five or six board members using existing staff from government departments. That is nonsense. It is as inane as the speech we heard from the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) during the debate leading to the setting up of the Anti-Inflation Board when he said the board would remain a small agency employing about 200 people. As we all know, by the spring of 1978 the staff of the AIB had grown to more than 1,000. And it didn't work. It didn't work then, and it certainly cannot work today.
Let us get back to those imported cauliflowers, to those lettuce imported from Holland. How about those tomatoes, those grapefruit? The hon. member may laugh, but these are one of the biggest factors in the jump in food prices over the last few months. Would a Canadian government board be able to arrive at the truth when examining the chain of items accounting for the high cost of imported food? Even if it did, would it be able to do anything about it? I cannot believe that even the members of the New Democratic Party take the view that it could. It would be powerless in respect of these imported items and, this being the case, it would become nothing more than a phony facade behind which the real culprit in this whole mess, the present government with its lack of fiscal and economic policy, could hide and take shelter.
Let me take hon. members back to a debate which took place on September 13, 1973. Speaking in this House in a debate on food policy, the hon. member for Oshawa-Whitby (Mr. Broadbent) said, and I quote him, that controls had been "an utter disaster" and that wherever they had been tried they had failed. They were, he said, merely a "convenient political gimmick." I say to you, sir, that the NDP motion before the House today is precisely that. It is a convenient political gimmick because, if they cannot nationalize a thing, they want to set up another board to oversee it. That is their answer to everything.

There is one thing I can honestly say I have not heard from them. They have not advocated setting up "FoodCan" or "GroceryCan" in an effort to control the industry.
What is the cause of the high prices of almost everything which is imported-food, cars, energy, textiles? Don't take my word for it, let's see what the latest of these ineffective expensive boards and commissions that both the government and the NDP are so fond of setting up, says. Within the last few days the Centre for the Study of Inflation and Productivity said in its own publication, "The Monitor":
Canada has experienced more inflation because of the depreciation (of the Canadian dollar). By the end of 1978, the CPI was 6V: per cent higher than it

Unfair Price Increases
would have been without the dollar depreciation. So the dollar decline has been responsible for about one-third of the total inflation measured by the CPI in this two-year period. In 1978 the CPI rose 9.0 per cent from the year before. Without depreciation of the dollar the increase would have been about 6 per cent.
Liberal member after Liberal member can rise in his place and say, as we heard earlier today, that the fall of the dollar- Canada's sinking dollar, not Canada's floating dollar-is a good thing for Canadians. Because of the large amount of imported foods, imported goods and imported materials we have to import, the drop in the dollar has added one-third, on the average, to the total inflation from which this country is suffering. Those cauliflowers, those tomatoes, that lettuce and that grapefruit would have had one-third cut off their normal seasonal price increase if Canada's dollar had remained constant.
What would another board or commission be able to do about the dollar's drop? Would it roll back the value of the dollar to parity or to where it should be? Would it prosecute the Government of Canada for imposing high taxes, causing loss of investor confidence, the high cost of government, the bungling of an inept Minister of Finance (Mr. Chretien) or the inability of the Prime Minister to control his bureaucracy or his policies, all of which have added to this country's shaky dollar dropsy? Of course, no Canadian board or commission would be able to do that. Earlier today we heard from the Lord High Poobah of economic ministers. His post was set up, I suspect, because the Prime Minister really did not have the political courage to fire the Minister of Finance. The President of the Board of Economic Development Ministers (Mr. Andras) says that CSIP is going to have increased monitoring powers. Big deal! With all the force I can muster I say that tinkering with government commissions and playing around with government boards will not cure the illness the government has caused in this country. Substituting a board or commission for the work and jurisdiction of an incredibly weak Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs (Mr. Allmand) also will not do it. The only answer is a clean, fresh broom.

Mr. Speaker, as I rise in the closing minutes of this interesting debate I must first make some reference to the closing remarks of the hon. member for Northumberland-Durham (Mr. Lawrence). He spoke about illnesses in the economy, and I think we all accept that there are certain areas, particularly unemployment, where indeed we do have

problems. We recognize that, but the hon. member talks about illnesses, and his financial spokesman recommends a deficit which would be 50 per cent greater than the one we already have. The hon. member did not tell us about what that would do to our balance of payments and to our exchange rate.
It was interesting to hear from the hon. member for York-Simcoe (Mr. Stevens) tonight. The hon. member seems to have toned down somewhat with regard to an increased deficit. He tells us now that he is not in favour of higher deficits. Other financial critics are, but he is not. He indicated earlier that he is quite happy with a 2 per cent growth rate. He commended the British Labour government for realizing the kind of growth rate it can expect in coming years. Earlier today he was criticizing Canada for having achieved a 3.4 per cent growth rate last year. However, that is typical of the varying opinions we hear from time to time from the variety club of five financial critics opposite.
The basic subject of the debate which has been going on here today has been the matter of inflation and its effect on families. We on this side obviously welcome such a debate because in recent years inflation has been an overriding concern of this government. The policies of the government have been directed toward bringing it under control while minimizing the adjustment costs to the economy.
We all recognize that there have been some setbacks, chiefly the result of elements beyond our domestic control, but they are being met and overcome. We still have a long, hard haul ahead, but this is a time for confidence and not gloom. In fact I believe that a mounting sense of confidence is now apparent in our economy, if not on the benches opposite.
I would like to move for a moment to the matter of food prices because I think that is the paramount issue on the minds of Canadians at this time, bearing in mind that the big increase in the rate of inflation last year was due in large part to increases in food prices. The hon. member for Nickel Belt (Mr. Rodriguez) referred earlier to increases in wages, and 1 think it should be noted that increases in the non-food sector were about in line with average figures for the increases in wages he mentioned.
Food prices are extremely sensitive to increased costs for energy, transportation and labour. The rate of increase in the total cost of living for non-food items has been considerably less than for food and has been trending downward until very recently. At the same time, over-all increases in average annual wage settlements have been on a distinct upward trend. As a result, the number of hours of work required to feed a family has continued to decrease remarkably. Recent price increases, though substantial in percentage terms, are less striking in terms of actual dollar costs for average annual consumption. The present upward movement in prices does not reflect a general pattern of profiteering by farmers, producers or retailers. On the contrary, no element of the food system has secured a rate of return higher than its historic average. Some of these points were made earlier this afternoon in the address by the President of the Board of Economic Development Ministers (Mr. Andras), but some of them need to be repeated.

More than one-third of the rate of increase in food prices reflects cyclical shortages in certain products, weather conditions and crop failures which are unusual and unavoidable.
Another third of the rate of increase in food prices reflects, as has been mentioned earlier today, the devaluation of the Canadian dollar, reductions in subsidies as a result of government restraint and supply management directed at ensuring reliable and stable domestic sources of supply, all of which are policies with more than offsetting advantages to Canadians in terms of increased employment, reductions in government expenditures and sound markets.
While the causes of increased food prices are therefore defensible and unavoidable, the government has been concerned about protecting the poor and the aged from their effects. To this end the government has modified the child tax credit program and increased the guaranteed income supplement in addition to the protection already afforded by indexing to these groups and to recipients of unemployment insurance and social assistance. Further measures to deal with food price increases are under review, but the government is determined to avoid steps which, in order to achieve allusory short-term improvements, in fact add to the bureaucracy, create inefficiencies, build in unacceptable longer-term costs, and simply tend to shift price burdens for consumers from one visible area to other less visible ones.
With regard to profits in food and beverages processing compared with all manufacturing for the years 1975 to 1978 there are a few points which perhaps should be registered. Food industry profits as a percentage of sales are lower than for all manufacturing. If the alcoholic beverage industry is deleted, the Department of Consumer and Corporate Affairs estimates the profits to be 4 per cent of sales, which is slightly higher than the 3.3 per cent estimated by the AIB for the first three-quarters of 1978. Profits as a percentage of equity for all manufacturers vary slightly from those of food and beverage processors. From the low point in 1976 the ratio of profits to equity in all manufacturing grew by 20.7 per cent, while that for food and beverages grew by only 13.4 per cent. For retailing, AIB sample data can be compared with Statistics Canada data for 1975 through 1977.

Recently the executive of CSIP wrote to the major coprorations for additional information on cost and prices to expand its work of analysis.
Hon. members will recall the decision taken a year ago with federal and provincial governments to hold down the growth of their spending below the growth rate of GNP. Again I want to repeat that the premier of Saskatchewan, a staunch member of the NDP, was not in favour of any stronger mechanism than the type of organization that was brought into effect with CSIP in this area, and I think it is important that federal members of the NDP appreciate that point.
The President of the Treasury Board (Mr. Buchanan) presented his main estimates for the Fiscal year which begins next April 1.
